REFLECTING within myself (*Most upright Augustine, you who through your zeal for benevolence have bound me to you in eternal gratitude*) with what service, with what mark of honor, with what pledge, or with what elaborate work of the intellect I might express this respect of my soul to you, it was my intent to honor you with some pure and great gift (*since you are worthy of the purest and greatest*), and to present certain books, composed as much with the elegant perfection of reason as with the rich value of matters, and a most dignified weight of maxims <term>maxims|The original Dutch "zin-spreuken" refers to pithy statements or aphorisms meant to impart deep moral or philosophical truths</term>, drawn from the innermost kernels of both Divine and Human...

<note>original: "zeer van nooden"</note> very much needs: However, so that I do not appear unmindful of your Excellency, while I am unable to present you with gifts worthy of you—those expansive offerings drawn from the treasures of the Sciences—at least from this, my shop of ignorance and indignation, I dedicate to you, as a token of my respect toward you, this *Cynical Oration* <note>The word "Cynic" comes from the Greek word for "dog." <meta>This page completes the sentence from the previous page, where Agrippa describes himself as a leader for those of the Divine Sciences. ...of Sciences, striving toward the **Fortress of Truth**. Receive then now, duty-bound friend *Augustine* <note>Augustine Scarpinel, a friend and patron of Agrippa.</note>, this ***Oration*** for what it is, and hold and keep it as you please; though I know, if you love ***huntsmen*** and ***dogs***, it cannot be anything but pleasant to you <note>Agrippa continues the metaphor of the "Cynic" (the dog-philosopher). He suggests that if his patron enjoys hunting for truth, he will appreciate this "barking" book.</note>.

But I, from being a ***Dog***, shall now move into a ***Crocodile***, or ***Dragon***, or some other fire-breathing ***Serpent***, and promptly complete the ***Description of Fire*** <note>original: "Vuur-beschrijving." This likely refers to a treatise on alchemy or pyromancy that Agrippa was working on simultaneously, or perhaps a section of his work on occult philosophy.</note> (a work such as our century has not yet seen, but useful only to a notorious ***World-destroyer***); then I will sprinkle myself with ***Holy Water***, and wash myself with ***running water***, by which I, having finally cast off these grim ***masks***, shall turn into a human again; so that, if I should circle about too much in a ***Pythagorean*** manner <term>Pythagorean: a reference to the doctrine of metempsychosis, or the transmigration of souls into different animal bodies</term> and inhabit so many terrifying animals, I might not at last, like ***Lucian*** and ***Apuleius***, be changed into a ***philosophical Ass*** <note>Lucian and Apuleius both wrote famous tales about men transformed into donkeys (The Golden Ass). Agrippa famously ends this book with a "Praise of the Ass," symbolizing the humble, simple believer who is superior to the proud, "wise" scholar.</note>.

But you now, live most happily, and remember, as you read this our work, *that to know nothing is the happiest life.* <note>original: "dat niet te weten, is, het allergelukkigste Leven." This is a translation of the Latin phrase "Nihil scire felicissima vita," a sentiment Agrippa borrows from the Greek playwright Sophocles to summarize his skeptical stance on human knowledge.</note>

<meta>This page follows the introductory dedication to Augustine Scarpinel. Having concluded his playful warning about turning into a "philosophical ass," Agrippa now begins his formal address "To the Reader," establishing the combative and revolutionary tone of the work by comparing his critique of the sciences to the Labors of Hercules.</meta>

# HEINRICH CORNELIUS
## A G R I P P A

->To the<-

# R E A D E R .

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'S' featuring scrolling acanthus leaves and floral patterns.</image-desc>
SHALL it not, diligent Reader, seem to you a magnanimous 
and overbold, indeed almost Hercu-
lean undertaking, to take up arms against this entire 
War of the Giants <note>original: "Reuzenkrijg." In Greek mythology, the Gigantomachy was a battle where giants attempted to overthrow the gods. Agrippa uses this to describe the massive, entrenched power of the academic establishment.</note> of all Sciences and 
Arts, and to challenge all those unrefined hunters of the same into the field? 
Against me shall snort the arrogance of the Teachers, the 
<margin>Licentiates.</margin> † bondage <note>original: "geheng," suggesting the constraints or rigid frameworks of the law.</note> of the learning of the Legal-counselors, the authority of the Masters, the endeavor of the Laureates, the zeal of all school-plodders <note>original: "school-stamperen," a derogatory term for those who mindlessly repeat scholastic lessons without thinking.</note>, and the rebellion of the Craftsmen: whom, if I strike them down, will it not be as much, indeed more, than slaying the Nemean Lion with a club? Destroying the Serpent of Lerna <note>the Hydra</note> with fire, killing the Eryman-
thian Boar, capturing the Hind with golden horns 
in the Maenalian Forest, shooting the Stymphal-
ian Birds in the clouds with arrows, 
squeezing Antaeus between the arms, 
planting pillars in the Sea, conquering the three-bodied Geryon, 
driving away the Oxen, slaying the Bull, 
overpowering Achelous in the wrestling match, 
carrying away the Horses of Diomedes, dragging Cerberus bound by a chain, 
stealing the golden apples of the Hesperides, and similar...

<summary>Agrippa introduces his work as a "Herculean" task, explicitly challenging the authority of all academic and professional disciplines. He lists the Twelve Labors of Hercules as a metaphor for the intellectual struggle he is initiating against the "Giants" of the established sciences.</summary>
<keywords>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Hercules, Labors of Hercules, academic critique, legal scholars, scholasticism, Giants, mythology</keywords>

# HEINRICH CORNELIUS
## A G R I P P A

<meta>The text continues the sentence from the previous page regarding the labors of Hercules.</meta>

...more, those which were accomplished by Hercules with great labor and no less danger? Since it is of no less difficulty, and of very great peril, to overcome these monsters of the schools of dispute and the arenas of combat; for do I not see what a bloody battle I have before me, and what a war full of danger, being hemmed in by an army of such mighty enemies: Oh! with how many engines of war will they resist me, with how many preparations will they attack me, with how many labels of infamy will they pursue me! First and foremost, those lousy Letter-nibblers <note>original: "Letterknabbelaars." A derogatory term for pedantic grammarians who obsess over the minutiae of language rather than its meaning.</note> will rush against me, and with their etymologies <note>original: "oorsprongk-leidingen."</note>, derive the name Agrippa from *Podagra* <note>Gout of the foot. Agrippa is mocking how grammarians use false linguistic origins to insult their enemies.</note>; the startled Poets will portray me as a Momus <note>the Greek god of satire and mockery, often used to represent a carping critic.</note>, or an Aesopic Goat in their poems; the trifle-torturing Historians will loathe me more than Pausanias <note>the assassin of Philip II of Macedon.</note> and Herostratus <note>who famously burned the Temple of Artemis to achieve immortal infamy.</note>; the grandiloquent Orators, with angry eyes, terrifying countenances, thunder-booming voices, and biting buffoonery, will accuse me of treason; the combative Disputants will shoot countless arrows of syllogisms <note>original: "sluitredenen," the formal logical arguments used in medieval scholasticism.</note> at me; the speech-flexible 

<margin>Sophists.</margin>

† Word-splitters <note>original: "Woord-vitters."</note>, with word-nooses and inextricable knots, will entangle me as if with a collar thrown about my neck: the wild Lullist <note>a follower of the "Great Art" of Ramon Llull, a complex system of logic that Agrippa elsewhere characterizes as a deceptive shortcut to knowledge.</note> will empty my head with uncontained words and disjointed reasons: the misshapen Memory-imprinters <note>original: "Geheug-inprenters," those who taught artificial memory systems or "mnemonics," which were highly popular but often seen as grotesque or unnatural.</note> will stomp the brains into me with crude grimaces; the godless Mathematicians will banish me from Heaven and Earth; the indivisible-writing Calculators, riling up the Usurers against me, will press me for the payment of debts: even to the...

<meta>This page continues Agrippa's preface "To the Reader." After listing the scholars and orators who will attack him, he now turns his satirical gaze toward the practitioners of the arts, sciences, and occult trades, predicting how each will use their specific craft to punish him for his critique of their "vanity."</meta>

...the irritable Gambler <note>original: "Dobbelaar." Likely referring to practitioners of Cleromancy (divination by dice) as much as common gamblers.</note> will condemn me to the gallows; the fate-telling Pythagorist <note>A follower of Pythagoras; here referring to numerologists who believe numbers govern fate.</note> will summon up unlucky numbers against me; the circle-dotting Geomancer <note>original: "Aard-konstenaar," literally "Earth-artist." One who practices divination by interpreting markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil.</note> will object with threats of imprisonment and sorrow, citing unlucky omens. The many-toned Musicians shall sing new songs of mockery about me for the common folk at every crossroads; and with the grinding of feet, and the discordant sounds of trumpets, cymbals, and metal spoons <note>original: "lepel-bletten." This refers to a "Charivari" or "rough music," a folk custom of making a loud, cacophonous noise to humiliate someone.</note>—making more noise than is customary at the weddings of widows and widowers—they shall make me perish in hearing and sight.

The magnificent Ladies shall hiss me out of their dance-circles; the plump Maidens will refuse me their kisses; and the gossiping Maidservants will mock me as if I were a dancing Camel <note>A contemporary metaphor for someone trying to perform an art for which they are physically or temperamentally unsuited; a clumsy oaf.</note>. The leaping Jester will, in a shameful conclusion, perform a tragicomedy about my life. The hundred-handed Fencer will strike at me from the left and the right. The confounded Geometricians, casting triangles and squares at me, shall take me prisoner as if I were tangled in a snare of Gordian knots.

The vain Perspective-painter shall depict and carve my likeness to be uglier than an Ape—yes, even uglier than Thersites <note>In Greek mythology, Thersites was a soldier of the Greek army during the Trojan War, famed for being the ugliest man there and a foul-mouthed critic of his leaders.</note> himself. The wild Geographers <note>original: "Wereld-meters," literally "World-measurers."</note> shall banish me further than the Sauromatians <note>An ancient nomadic people of the Eurasian steppe; used here to represent the most remote and desolate edge of the known world.</note> and the icy North. The Daedalian Architect <note>referencing Daedalus, the mythical craftsman who built the Labyrinth of Crete.</note> shall secretly lock me in inescapable structures and, once I am caught, force me to wander in incomprehensible labyrinths. The hellish Miner <note>original: "Metaal-graver," referring to both miners and alchemists who "dig" into the nature of metals.</note> shall consign me to the subterranean gold mines. The deadly Astrologers <note>original: "Starrekijkers," literally "Star-gazers."</note> shall threaten me with the rope <note>original: "bast," meaning the inner bark of a tree or hemp fiber used to make a hangman's noose.</note>, and through the revolving rotation of the Heavens, they will seek to prevent my ascent to the blessed ranks. Finally, the threatening Diviners shall predict every possible calamity for my future.

<meta>Catchword: ze. ### To the Reader.

the **Peripatetics** ‡ <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they discussed philosophy while walking (peripatountes).</note> shall fool my soul to death, and whistle me out of Paradise; the strict **Stoics** * <note>Followers of Zeno, known for their belief that virtue is based on knowledge and that one should be indifferent to pleasure and pain.</note>, stripping me of all human inclinations, shall turn me into a flint-stone; the high-snoring **Metaphysicians** <term>Metaphysics: the branch of philosophy that examines the fundamental nature of reality, including the relationship between mind and matter.</term> will never cease with paradoxes, as if from the **Demogorgonian** <note>Demogorgon was a mysterious deity of the underworld, often associated with primordial chaos.</note> **carillon** † <note>original: "Beijaard," a set of bells; the author uses it here to describe a clanging, chaotic jumble.</note> of things that are nowhere, nor ever shall be, to make me lose my wits; the moralizing **Disciplinarians** will point me to the hundred tables of the Laws; the **Civil Lawgiver** will deny me public office; the **voluptuous Prince** will forbid me the Court; the **ambitious Rulers** will bar me from their public feasts; the **bitter People** will prick me with insults along the street; a terrible practitioner of violence, **Phalaris** <note>A cruel tyrant of Acragas in Sicily, famous for the "Brazen Bull," a torture device in which victims were roasted alive.</note>, will shut me in his **Bull** to be tortured; the **conspiring Usurpers** will send me into exile; the **unruly Rabble**, that many-headed wicked beast, will—without reason—drag me to my ruin; every **desperate Democracy** will suspect me of treason; the **greedy Priests** will drive me from the altars; the **disguised Cowls** <note>Refers to monks, named for the hoods (cowls) of their habits.</note> and scornful **Hypocrites** will snarl at me from the pulpit; the **sovereign Popes** will reserve my sins for the eternal fire; the **sprightly Whores** will threaten me with the **Spanish itch** <note>A common historical euphemism for syphilis, which was often blamed on neighboring nations.</note>; the **cunning Ruffian** and **spider-like Procuress** will seek to cut my purse; the **scurvy Beggars** will shut me out of the infirmary; the **vagrant Thieves** will call down the **holy fire** <note>Likely referring to St. Anthony’s Fire (Ergotism or Erysipelas), a painful skin condition.</note> and a **furious bite** <note>Potentially a reference to rabies.</note> upon me, and being frustrated by their indulgences—

‡ Followers of Aristotle. * Followers of Zeno. † Chaos.

<meta>This page continues Agrippa's introductory address "To the Reader." Having previously listed the various professional classes that will likely attack him for his skepticism toward their "sciences," he now explains his true motivation: defending the simplicity of faith against the arrogance of human philosophy and the rigid dogmatism of the universities.</meta>

# Henrik Kornelis Agrippa.

...and, if it must be so, I who have willingly provoked so many enemies against myself, shall gladly let my life fall to pieces rather than abandon my position. I want you to know that I have not written this out of hatred, nor ambition, nor malice, nor because I was carried away by error. No sacrilegious desire, no arrogance of an ungodly mind has driven me to this, but rather the most just and true cause of all: namely, that I see many who are so conceited in their human teachings and sciences *that they—because the concise sayings of the Holy Scriptures and the <margin>Canonical</margin> inspired writings of the Holy Spirit supposedly lack the ornaments of words, the power of syllogisms <note>logical arguments where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>, the most attractive rhetoric, and the exotic learning of the <margin>Philosophers</margin>; and because they are established simply in the practice of virtue and pure faith—treat these scriptures as if they were boorish and ignorant, not only despising and scorning them, but even persecuting them as worthless.*

Others we see—though they seem to themselves to be quite a bit more pious—who indeed attempt to praise and uphold the laws of Christ, yet they grant more authority to the decrees of the philosophers than to God's Holy Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles, even though the latter differ from the former more than day from night. Furthermore, in many, indeed almost all schools <note>original: "oeffenplaatsen," referring to the universities or academies of the time</note>, this harmful manner and damnable custom has taken root: that they force the novice students to promise by oath to bind themselves to Aristotle, or Boethius, or Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, or Albert <note>Albertus Magnus</note>, or some othe...

<meta>catchword: ren (forming "anderen" / "others")</meta>

<summary>Agrippa defends his motives for writing, arguing that he is not driven by malice but by a desire to challenge those who value human philosophy and academic authorities like Aristotle over the simplicity of the Holy Scriptures.</summary>

<keywords>skepticism, Holy Scripture vs. Philosophy, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Boethius, Albertus Magnus, scholasticism, academic oaths, religious authority</keywords>

--- Page 25 ---
<meta>This page concludes the preface "To the Reader." Agrippa continues his critique of the academic establishment, specifically focusing on the dogmatic worship of classical authorities (like Aristotle) and the way universities stifle intellectual and spiritual freedom in favor of human-made traditions.</meta>

## To the Reader.

...of never contradicting their **Scholarly Idol**; from whom, if anyone should think even a hair-breadth differently, they are denounced as a shameful **Heretic**, as an offense to pious ears, and as one who must be destroyed with fire and flame. These frivolous **Braggarts** <note>original: "Snorkers," meaning loud boasters or blowhards</note> and enemies of the **Holy Scriptures** I must now confront. I must attack their armies and fortresses by demonstrating how great human blindness is, and how, through so many **sciences** and **arts**—along with the many masters and inventors of each—men continually wander away from the knowledge of the **Truth**. 

And oh! what frivolity, what audacious delusion! To place the schools of the **Philosophers** <note>original: "Wijf-geren," a Dutch term literally meaning "seekers of wisdom"</note> above the **Church of Christ**, and the opinions of men above or alongside the **Word of God**. Finally, what an ungodly exercise of force it is to lead the minds of newcomers <note>referring to students entering the university</note> captive to the aforementioned "inventors," and to strip the pupils of their **freedom** to seek out and follow the truth for themselves. Since all these things are so clear that no denial is possible, I must be granted leave if I seem to speak a bit more boldly, or perhaps a bit more sharply, against certain types of academic disciplines and their primary promoters.

->Farewell.<-

### Henrik Kornelis Agrippa.

...and, if it must be, I who have willingly raised so many enemies against myself, will gladly see my life broken in pieces rather than abandon my post. This I want you to know: that I have not written this being carried away by hate, nor by ambition, nor by deceit, nor by error; no sacrilegious desire, no arrogance of an unpious mind has driven me to this, but rather the most righteous and truest cause of all—namely, that I see that many are so conceited in their human teachings and sciences that they therefore—because they supposedly lack the decorations of words, the power of syllogisms, the very attractive persuasions, and the foreign learning of the † **Philosophers** <note>original: "Wijs-geeren," literally 'seekers of wisdom'</note>; and because they are simply sustained by the working of virtue and by pure faith—not only despise and disdain the aphorisms of the **Holy Scriptures** and the \* **canonical** <note>original: "ingelüste," meaning inspired or accepted into the official canon of the Bible</note> writings of the **Holy Spirit** as if they were boorish and ignorant, but even persecute them with further indignity. We see others who, although they seem quite a bit more pious to themselves, do indeed attempt to praise and confirm **Christ’s Laws**, yet they grant more authority to the decrees of the **Philosophers** than to God’s **Holy Prophets**, **Evangelists**, and **Apostles**, even though these differ from those more than day and night. Furthermore, in many—indeed, in almost all—**places of learning** <note>original: "oeffenplaatsen," referring to the universities or academic gymnasiums of the time</note>, this harmful manner and damnable custom has penetrated: they make the newly beginning students promise by oath to bind themselves to **Aristotle**, or **Boethius**, or **Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, the influential medieval theologian</note>, or **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus, a prominent German Dominican friar and philosopher</note>, or some other—

---

\* **Canonical**. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; † **Philosophers**.

He specifically condemns the university practice of forcing students to swear allegiance to specific scholastic authorities like Thomas Aquinas or Aristotle.</summary>

### Henrik Kornelis Agrippa's
# Declamation
#### Of the
### Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences and Arts.

---

*Of the Sciences in General.*

### Chapter I.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'I' featuring intricate foliage and scrolled patterns.</image-desc> It is an old opinion, and the nearly unanimous and singular judgment of almost all philosophers <term>Wijsgerigen</term> <note>Literally "wisdom-seekers"; the author refers to the classical Greek and Roman philosophical tradition.</note>, that every science <term>wetenschap</term> <note>In this period, "science" refers to any branch of formal learning or knowledge, including the humanities, and not just the natural sciences.</note> bestows something divine upon man himself, according to the understanding and worth of each; so much so that through it, he can often raise himself beyond the limits of humanity into the ranks of the more blessed gods. From this have arisen those various and countless panegyrics of the sciences, with which everyone attempts to show off—with a discourse no less elegant than it is long—and exalt even above heaven itself those arts <term>konsten</term> <note>Refers to the "Liberal Arts," the core curriculum of medieval and Renaissance education.</note> and teachings in which they have sharpened the powers of their mind through daily practice. But I, persuaded by reasons of a completely different nature, judge that nothing can be more harmful and nothing more poisonous to the life of men and the welfare of our souls than these very arts and sciences: therefore it seems

<summary>This page serves as the title page and introduction to Chapter 1 of Agrippa's skeptical masterpiece. He introduces his core argument: contrary to the common belief that knowledge makes men god-like, he contends that the arts and sciences are actually harmful to human life and the soul.</summary>

<keywords>Henrik Kornelis Agrippa, Declamation, Uncertainty and Vanity, Philosophy, Sciences and Arts, Skepticism, Renaissance thought</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Chapter I. The previous page ended with the phrase "therefore it seems," which this page completes as "to me that I must begin..."</meta>

#### Of the Uncertainty and Vanity,

to me that I must begin with a completely opposite arrangement; it is my opinion that one ought not only to refrain from praising the sciences with such descriptions, but rather to a large extent to revile them, and that there is not a single one that can escape the just punishment of reproach; and again, not one that deserves any praise of itself, unless it should borrow some from the integrity <term>onbesprokenheyd</term> <note>Literally "unspoken-of-ness," implying a reputation so clean it leaves no room for gossip; blamelessness.</note> of its professors. However, I wish for this opinion of mine to be accepted by you with such modesty that you do not think I intend to coerce others who feel differently, or to willfully claim anything for myself. Therefore, you shall grant me leave—I who differ from others in this—until we have discussed this opinion regarding all the (a) faculties <margin>(a) *Faculties.*</margin>, in alphabetical order: not merely with common arguments taken from the appearance of things, but produced with concise reasons from the very innermost bowels <note>A common Renaissance metaphor meaning the deep, essential core of a subject.</note> of the matters; not with the argument-heavy eloquence of *Demosthenes* <note>The most famous orator of ancient Greece, known for his powerful political speeches.</note> or *Chrysippus* <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his intricate, sometimes pedantic logic and dialectic skills.</note>, which would bring shame to me, a professor of the Holy Scriptures, being a sign of flattery to wish to follow the cosmetic flourishes <term>blanketselen</term> <note>Literally "face paints" or "whitening agents"; a metaphor for artificial rhetorical decorations that hide the truth.</note> in speech: for a follower of the Holy Scriptures must properly consider the speaking, not the ornate speaking, and the truth of the matter, not the decoration of the argument: for the dwelling place of truth is not on the tongue, but in the heart: it matters not, in speaking truth, what kind of reasoning we use: for deceitful speech has need of flowery words, so that it may overpower the minds of men: but the word of truth (as *Euripides* <note>A famous Greek playwright; Agrippa frequently cites classical authorities to dismantle the very intellectual traditions they represent.</note> says) is simple, seeking no adornments nor

<summary>Agrippa begins his critique by arguing that the sciences deserve reproach rather than praise. He declares his intention to examine every academic faculty in alphabetical order, favoring simple, heart-felt truth over the deceptive, ornate rhetoric of classical orators.</summary>

<keywords>critique of science, rhetoric vs truth, Demosthenes, Chrysippus, Holy Scriptures, Euripides, academic faculties, vanity of learning</keywords>

# Of the Uncertainty and Vanity,

evil spirit <note>The text completes the previous page's sentence: "Let him [be considered the author], that evil spirit..."</note>, who first devised the sciences which are as much harmful as they are beneficial; just as *Thamus*, King of *Egypt* <note>A reference to a story in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where King Thamus argues that the invention of writing will weaken human memory.</note>, learnedly treated, concerning the inventors of the sciences and letters: from this it follows that most letter-nibblers <note>original: "letter-knabbelaars"; a derogatory term for pedantic grammarians.</note> explain the word *Demon* <note>original: "Demon [geest]"; from the Greek *daimōn*, which some etymologists linked to *daēmōn*, meaning "knowing" or "learned."</note> as "one who knows." But be that as it may—whether we leave these fictions to the poets and philosophers or believe that the sciences were found by men—we nevertheless know that these inventors were children of a wicked generation; children, I say, of Cain: and of whom it is truly said, 

> *The children of this world*
> *are more prudent in this generation, than the chil-*
> *dren of light.* <note>Luke 16:8.</note>

If then the inventors of the sciences are men, is not every man a liar? <note>Psalm 116:11.</note> There is none who does good, no, not one: but even assuming some men are good, the sciences themselves can derive no goodness nor truth from that, except for what they borrow and obtain from the inventors themselves, or the practitioners: for if they happen to fall upon an evil person, they shall be harmful, and shall make him from bad to even worse. Thus [the sciences] turn the Grammarian <note>original: "Letter-knabbelaar."</note> perverse, the Poet into an idle-talker, the Historian into a liar, the Orator into a flatterer <note>original: "pluimstrijker"; literally "one who strokes feathers."</note>, the Chronicler <note>original: "Onthoud-schrijver"; literally "memory-writer."</note> into a boaster, the Logician <note>original: "Redenkaveler."</note> into a quarrelsome person, the Sophist <note>original: "Woord-vitter"; literally "word-picker."</note> into a confuser, the Lullist <note>original: "Lullist"; a follower of the "Great Art" of Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), which used logical diagrams to seek universal knowledge.</note> into a babbler, the Magician <note>original: "Zelkonstenaar"; likely referring to a practitioner of celestial or natural magic.</note> into a fortuneteller, the Singer into a wanton, the Dancer into a shameless person, the Geometrician <note>original: "Meetkonstenaar."</note> into a braggart, the Geographer <note>original: "Werelt-beschrijver."</note> into a vagabond, the Archi-

A

<summary>The author argues that the sciences are inherently corrupt because they originated from a "wicked generation" (the lineage of Cain) and reflect the flaws of their human practitioners. He provides a list of various professions—from poets to geometricians—showing how their specific studies tend to amplify human vices rather than virtues.</summary>

<keywords>King Thamus, Cain, Demon, Ramon Llull, vices, Grammarians, Sophists, vanity of learning</keywords>

<header>*of Sciences and Arts.*</header>

In this way, the letters of the Hebrews were lost during the captivity in Babel, and their language was corrupted by the Chaldeans. Conversely, as the wheel of fortune turned, the letters and language of the Romans were in turn corrupted and changed by the Goths, Lombards, Franks, and other wild nations; for the Latin language of today is not the same as it was in the past. 

Even concerning the Hebrew language and script, there is no small disagreement even among the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> themselves. For Rabbi Jehuda says that *Adam*, the first-created man, spoke according to the (b) <margin>otherwise Scythian</margin> Aramaic idiom. # Of Uncertainty and Vanity

[...lying] are they, who trust most in their own precepts, and yet speak least correctly of all. For all right of speech consists not with the **letter-nibblers**, but with the people; and the usage of speaking well is polished by common custom. ### *Of Poetry.*
## CHAPTER IV.

Poetry itself, as *Quintilian* <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a Roman educator and rhetorician.</note> testifies, is the second part of grammar <term>letterkonst|Literally "the art of letters," which in a 16th-century context referred to the study of grammar, philology, and literary analysis.</term>. It is an art devised for no other end than to tickle the ears of foolish men with playful rhymes, with the meter and weight of syllables, and a vain jingle of words, and to lead minds astray with the pleasures of fables and the husks of lies. Therefore, it has deserved to be called the *Mistress of Lies* and the practitioner of false doctrines. And even if we allow her this much regarding her mad passion, buffoonery <note>original: "kobachtigheid," implying mimicry or acting like a jester.</note>, impudence, and audacity—certainly, who could endure such undaunted courage in lying with a good conscience? is: But let us return to historiography. Although this discipline most of all requires a continuity of events <note>original: "volgdraad," literally a "following thread" or chronological sequence.</note>, faithfulness, consistency, and truth, it nevertheless fulfills these least of all. Historians differ so greatly among themselves, and speak of the same things so entirely differently and variously, that it is impossible that many of them are not very deceitful. I speak not only of the *Creation of the World*, of the general *Flood* <note>The Great Deluge or Noah's Flood.</note>, or of the building of the *City of Rome*—from which chronological roots they claim to begin their history books—since they all know nothing of the first, do not all believe the second, and the third is uncertain among them. Therefore, since these things are long past and are not accepted with any uniformity by all, one may forgive them these errors. 

But regarding later times, the reproach of falsehood cannot be washed from them; yet the causes of this disagreement are manifold. For most, because they were not present at the times, places, persons, and actions of the narratives, follow common rumor based on the accounts of others, and thus describe nothing certain and nothing steadfast. ### Of Rhetoric.
## CHAPTER VI.

But Rhetoric, which comes next here, whether it be an art or not, is disputed by the most famous men; the case is still pending; *Socrates* himself asserts, in *Plato*, with concise arguments, that it is neither an art nor a science, but a certain cleverness, which in itself is neither noble nor honest, but rather a shameful, unfree, and slavish sycophancy: *Lysias*, *Cleanthes*, and *Menedemus* have felt that eloquence cannot be defined by any art, but that it arises only from nature, which teaches everyone, when necessary, to flatter, to present their case, and to confirm the same with persuasive arguments; and that pure pronunciation, memory, and the ingenuity of invention arise from nowhere else but nature, which was evident even in *Antonius* <note>Marcus Antonius (143–87 BCE), a Roman orator and grandfather of Mark Antony, who claimed his eloquence was natural rather than learned.</note>, a Prince of *Roman* orators: and it is evident that, since no one before *Tisias*, *Corax*, and *Gorgias* <note>The traditional founders of Greek rhetoric in the 5th century BCE.</note> had described or taught *Rhetoric*, there were nevertheless very eloquent people through the skill of their own wit. # Of the Uncertainty and Vanity

The Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans, known for their "laconic" or brief speech, who valued action over words.</note> banished Ctesiphon <note>A Greek orator who famously proposed a gold crown for Demosthenes; he was criticized here for his excessive loquacity.</note> (because he boasted that he could speak for an entire day on any given subject): for among them, nothing was more hateful than that precise artifice of the tongue of those who do not even pay attention to speaking the truth. Instead, presenting a mediocre work, they seek to decorate it with the **whore’s cosmetics of discourse** <note>original: "hoereblanketselen des vertoogs" — a vivid metaphor for the deceptive ornamentation and "makeup" used by orators to hide the truth.</note> and the **pompousness of words**, and by the sweetness of speaking, to deceive the minds of the listeners. Binding the eyes of the audience to themselves, they lead them around by the ears. 

And it is now evident that no one has become better through this artifice, but many have become worse; we see that although they know how to speak briefly of the Virtues, they are nonetheless more outstanding and possess a more powerful eloquence in defending errors, in sowing strife, in stirring up disagreements, and in stirring up heaps of insults, slanders, and blasphemies, rather than in establishing peace, harmony, and rest, or in impressing love, loyalty, and Religion. 

Furthermore, many who give themselves over to this cleverness have deviated from the true faith: divisions and schisms, superstitions and heresies have been hatched from this; while some so despise the Holy Scripture—because it lacks eloquence and **Ciceronian elegance** <note>Referring to the refined, complex style of Marcus Tullius Cicero, which was the academic standard for Latin oratory but was often contrasted with the "plain" style of the Bible.</note>—that with those decorated persuasions of pagan proof-making, they sometimes dare to feel against the universal truth. This is especially evident in the Tatianist <note>Followers of Tatian, a 2nd-century teacher who combined Greek philosophy with Christianity before being declared a heretic for his extreme asceticism.</note> heretics, and in those to whom Libanius <note>A 4th-century Greek teacher of rhetoric who remained a pagan despite the Christianization of the Roman Empire.</note> the word-splitter, and Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a prominent Roman statesman and orator who famously defended the traditional Altar of Victory against Christian emperors.</note> the orator...

# Of Uncertainty and Vanity,

## CHAPTER X.
### Of the Art of Memory.

TO these Arts is also added the <term>Art of Memory</term> <note>Also known as Mnemonics or the Method of Loci.</note>, which (as *Cicero* says) is nothing else than an introduction and manner of instruction consisting of places and images, acting as a writing tablet. It was first devised in the shorthand characters <note>original: *schrijfstrikken*. This refers to the mnemonic symbols or "notae" used to represent words.</note> of *Simonides of Ceos* <note>original: *Simonides Melito*. An ancient Greek lyric poet credited with inventing the art of memory after identifying victims of a collapsed building by where they had been sitting.</note> and later perfected by *Metrodorus of Scepsis*. This art, however—whatever it may be worth—can by no means exist without natural memory. Indeed, it often fills the natural memory with so many monstrous images that, instead of a sharp memory, it sometimes produces light-headedness and insanity; specifically, when it overloads the natural memory with countless images of things and words, it drives those who are not content with the boundaries of nature to madness through the art. Therefore, when *Simonides*, or someone else, offered this art to *Themistocles* <note>An Athenian general and politician known for his brilliant natural intellect.</note>, he replied: "I would rather have an art of forgetting, for I remember much that I do not wish to, and I cannot forget that which I want." And *Quintilian* says of *Metrodorus* that it was a matter of vanity and boasting for him to take more pride in his memory through art than through nature. Regarding this, *Cicero* has written in the *Book of New Orators* <note>original: *boek der nieuwe redenaren*. This refers to the *Rhetorica ad Herennium*, which in the Renaissance was widely (though incorrectly) attributed to Cicero.</note>; and *Quintilian* in his *Instructions* <note>original: *onderwijzingen*, referring to the *Institutio Oratoria*.</note>; and *Seneca*; and among the later writers, *Petrarch*, *Marullus of Verona*, *Peter of Ravenna* <note>Author of "The Phoenix" (1491), the most famous memory manual of the era.</note>, *Hermann von dem Busche*, and others.

<summary>This chapter critiques the "Art of Memory" (mnemonics), arguing that artificial systems of images and places can overburden the mind and lead to madness rather than true wisdom.</summary>

### CHAPTER XII.

->*Of the Pythagorean Lot.*<-

## CHAPTER XV.

In my judgment, one should not pass over what the **Pythagoreans** practiced, and, as others believe, what **Aristotle** himself believed: that the primary names of the letters have their own specific numbers, from which, using the proper names of men, predictions were made. The numbers of the letters of each person's name were gathered together; once collected, they ascribed victory to the one whose total exceeded the other, whether the matter being investigated was war, or peace, or a dispute, or marriage, or life, or any such thing. By this means, they say, **Patroclus** was defeated by **Hector**, and he in turn was overpowered by **Achilles**. **Terentianus** <note>Terentianus Maurus, a 2nd-century Latin grammarian who wrote on meters and letters.</note> confirms this in these verses; and the names, they say, were thus composed of these letters:

> *Let this consist of the greater, that of the lesser sum:*
> *To meet the wavering chance of war as it may come.*
> *Where the greatest number stood, victory showed its grace,*
> *The omen of death was plain, in the lowest number’s place:*

From this have sprouted the heresies of **Marcus the Magician** <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who applied numerical values to the alphabet to uncover "mysteries" in the name of God.</note> and **Valentinus**; established in numbers and grown out of numbers, these men claimed that they were able to discover the holy religion and countless secrets of Divine truth through these most foolish <note>The original Dutch *stommelachtigste* implies something that is not only stupid but senseless or clumsy.</note> numbers. To this is added the **Pythagorean** recantation <note>Likely referring to the *palinodia* or the secretive oaths of the Pythagorean school.</note> observed during initiations, and more such things, which are all vain, trifling, and false. For these arithmeticians, nothing true has remained but a difficult and lifeless number, and yet they believe that they lead a divine life simply because they are able to count; but the **Musicians** <term>musicians</term> <note>Original: *Maatzangers*, literally "measure-singers" or those who study rhythm and harmony.</note> are loath to grant them this credit, preferring to attribute this honor to their own melodious harmony.

# XVII. CHAPTER.

Let us now speak of *Music*; about which *Aristoxenus* <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who was one of the earliest to write extensively on music theory.</note> wrote at length among the Greeks, asserting that even the soul is *music*; whose doctrines *Boethius* <note>The 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard textbook on music for a thousand years.</note> afterwards handed down to the *Latins*: I speak now of this *music* which consists in the caressing of voices and sounds, not that which is called poetry—derived from the measures, rhymes, and fictions of poems—which, according to the testimony of *Alfarabi* <note>original: *Alfarabius*. A renowned medieval philosopher and music theorist of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>, is driven not so much by sensibility and reason as by a passionate frenzy, of which we have spoken above: but this music, which consists of temperaments <term>temperaments</term> <note>The adjustment of musical intervals to achieve harmony.</note>, which is a concord of strings and voices, sounding together in their measure without offending the ears; and it deals with sounds, with pauses, with connections, with the melodies <note>Dutch: *wijz*.</note>, with the modulations <note>Dutch: *verwálingen*.</note>, and with the rhythmic vibrations <term>neuritranzes</term> <note>Likely a corruption of a term referring to the mechanical movement or vibration of strings.</note>. The Ancients divided these into *Supraconsonant* <note>Original: *Opperovereentemmige*. Referring to the theoretical, mathematical music of the spheres.</note>, *ornamental*, and *practical*; yet they left aside the first (namely the *Supraconsonant*) because of its all too profound difficulty and its impossible experimental nature; and the second, they disdained and discarded out of a dislike for its fussiness <note>Original: *krieligheid*, implying triviality or excessive, distracting detail.</note>; but they admitted only the third kind (pretending that it resembled the structure of the world). ### *Of the Mimetic Dance.*
## XX. CHAPTER.

THE Mimetic dance <term>Mimetic dance: translated from "Kamerſpeelige dans," referring to theatrical pantomime where stories are told through gesture and movement without speech.</term> is an artifice of imitation and demonstration, which explains things conceived in the mind through an appropriate mimicry: representing all manners and inclinations so nakedly and openly that every spectator can easily understand the performer—even if he does not speak a word—from his many movements and gestures. Such is the power of this buffoonery <note>Original: "potsemaking," referring here to the art of the mime or jester.</note> that it has no need for interpreters at all. For it portrays a grandfather, a child, a woman, a servant, a maidservant, a drunkard, a wrathful man, and the various dispositions and inclinations of all men, with such a pleasant mimicry, so fittingly, that even the onlooker from afar, although he cannot hear the play, can understand its content solely from the expressions <note>Original: "mijnen," meaning facial expressions or mien.</note> of the performer. ### *Of Theatrical Dance.*

## Of Geometry.
### CHAPTER XXII.

*Geometry* itself, which the Jew *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note> calls the foremost and mother of all exercises, possesses this praise above all other disciplines: that whereas among the followers of almost all other arts there are great and innumerable quarrels, all *Geometers* everywhere agree with one another. Nor is there any other dispute among them, except that they split hairs <note>Original: *hairkloven*, to argue over minute details.</note> regarding points, lines, and surfaces: whether they are divisible or indivisible. Furthermore, they do not differ from one another in doctrine nor in tradition; rather, each man strives to surpass the others in new or more subtle discoveries which no one had ever thought of before. However, up to this day, not a single *Geometer* has found the squaring of the circle <note>Finding a square with the exact same area as a given circle, a famously impossible task using only a compass and straightedge.</note>, or provided a uniform line for a cube’s side <note>Likely referring to the "doubling of the cube" or the Delian problem, another classic unsolvable problem of ancient geometry.</note>, even though *Archimedes of Syracuse* once thought he had found it, and many descendants up to this time have somewhat attempted the same—though in vain—even if they seem to have come very close to it. ### *Of (a) Optics, or Perspective.* <note>Original: *Gezichtkonft, of de Doorfchouwing*. The author uses the Dutch term *Doorfchouwing* as a literal translation of the Latin *perspectiva*, meaning "looking through."</note>

## CHAPTER XXIII.

To Geometry, *Optics* is the closest neighbor, which they call *Perspective*; after that come *Cosmography* <note>Original: *Wereldmeting*, literally "world-measuring," referring to the mapping of the earth and heavens.</note> and *Architecture*. Now, *Perspective*, or *Optics*, treats these three kinds of vision: the *direct*, the *reflected*, and the *refracted* <note>These correspond to the classical divisions of optics: rectilinear propagation, catoptrics (mirrors), and dioptrics (lenses).</note>, and teaches what *light*, what *shadows*, and what *distances* are. It delves into the causes of visible things which appear false due to *distances*, and investigates the shooting of rays through one or more transparent things across various shapes of bodies. Furthermore, it demonstrates the images of shadows and light, and what attribute is caused by the objects themselves, what is caused by the sight, or what comes about by some accidental medium; also how objects and the sight, through the diversity of the medium, are outlined with different forms. 

For regarding the nature of vision, there are various and conflicting opinions: *Plato* believes that sight occurs through "illumination"—namely, that light which comes out of the eyes, shooting off into the external air, meets the light that comes from the bodies; and that the air in between is easily sifted and penetrated by the far-reaching, fiery power of the sight. *Galen* <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher whose views on anatomy and perception dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> feels in unison with *Plato*: But *Hipparchus* says that the rays cast out from the eyes to the bodies touch them just as

## Of the Art of Painting.
### Chapter XXIV.

THE Art of Painting is an imitative <note>Original: *wanschapene*. While this literally means "misshapen" or "deformed" in modern Dutch, here it refers to the art being a "counterfeit" or "artificial" imitation of nature, reflecting the author's skeptical view that such arts are distortions of reality.</note> art, yet very pure in the imitation of natural things, consisting of the *sketching* of the *outlines*, and a proper handling of colors; this art was formerly held in such high esteem that it held the first place among the *Liberal Arts* <note>Original: *Vrije konsten*. These were the academic disciplines—such as rhetoric, logic, and geometry—considered essential for a free citizen to master.</note>; for it is no less free than the *Art of Poetry*; just as *Flaccus* <note>The Roman poet Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus).</note> has very well sung,

> The painter’s paint has always had the power,
> As has the poet’s pen, to dare what they imagined.
> <note>A translation of the famous line from Horace's *Ars Poetica*: "Pictoribus atque poetis quidlibet audendi semper fuit aequa potestas."</note>

The *art of painting* is said to be nothing other than a silent *Poetry*, and *Poetry* a speaking painting, so closely are they related to one another; for just as the Poets do, so the Painters embellish histories and fables, and express the images of all things: *light*, *gloss*, *shadows*, *projections*, and *depressions* <note>Original: *neerdellingen*. In this context, it refers to the recessed or darker areas in a painting that provide depth, contrasting with the "projections" or highlights.</note>: furthermore, painting possesses this from the *Art of Sight* <note>Original: *Gezichtkonst*, referring to the science of optics.</note>, that it deceives the sight, and in an image of various perspectives, pours more forms into the eyes of the spectators: and that which *sculpture* cannot reach, this art attains; it paints *fire*, *rays*, *light*, *thunders*, *lightnings*,

Now it was also found by experience, as *Pliny* relates, that when the *Triumvirate* <note>Original: *Drieman-schap*. Moreover, the *Art of Painting* has this quality: that in all its works, more is always understood and judged than is seen within them, just as *Plutarch* <note>A Greek historian and biographer.</note> very diligently scrutinized in his portraits <note>Original: *beeldenissen*. Here referring to his vivid character descriptions or biographies.</note>; and though the Art may be very high, the intellect is nevertheless above the Art.

# Of *Sculpture*, and *Modeling*.
## CHAPTER XXV.

Painting is joined by *Sculpture* and *Modeling*, the *Art of Casting*, and the *Art of Engraving*—artifices of a rude wit <note>Original: *onbeschoft vernuft*. This refers to an unrefined or base intellect, as the author views these manual arts as spiritually dangerous.</note> which can nonetheless also be understood under the heading of *Architecture*. *Sculpture* creates the likenesses of things out of stone, wood, or ivory <note>Original: *elp*. An archaic Dutch term for ivory, derived from the word for elephant.</note>; *Modeling* fashions the same from a lump of clay; yet the art of casting expresses these in a mold <note>Original: *kneeding*. Literally "kneading" or "shaping," referring here to the process of forming the mold for metalwork.</note> made of copper and other metals: and the *engraver* carves them into stones and precious gems. On this subject, in later times, *Pomponius Gauricus* <note>An Italian Renaissance humanist (c. 1482–1530) who wrote a famous treatise titled *De Sculptura*.</note> has written: but all these arts, equally with the art of painting, I believe to have been devised by evil devils for the sake of ostentation <note>Original: *praalsnorking*. Meaning boastful display or empty pomp.</note>, lust, and superstition. These are they who first of all, according to the words of *Paul* <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul in Romans 1:23.</note>, *changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things*; they (contrary to the Divine commandment forbidding the making of any graven image or likeness, whether of things high in Heaven or low upon the earth) have introduced <term>idolatry</term> <note>Original: *beeldendienst*. Literally "image-service."</note>, which is so hateful to God. Of this the Wise Man <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Wisdom (often attributed to Solomon in the Apocrypha), specifically chapter 14.</note> says, *the image itself is cursed, and he that made it; and that which was made shall suffer torment: for the vanity of men, he says further, has found these arts for the temptation of the souls of men, and as a snare for fools: and the invention of them is the corruption of life.*

## CHAPTER XXVII.

Let us now further briefly survey *Cosmography*; this is now divided into *Geography* <note>original: *Wereldbeschrijving*, literally "World-description."</note> and *Chorography* <note>original: *Landbeschrijving*, literally "Land-description."</note>. Both measure and distinguish the World, but the first—according to the order of Celestial things—measures, by their own distinction, with a measure of (a) *degrees* and *minutes*, the locations of countries and places lying beneath them. It teaches the properties of the climates <note>latitudinal zones</note> and the differences between days and nights, the primary names of the winds, the various risings of the stars, the elevations of the (b) *Poles*, the parallels and meridians, the shadows of the sundials <note>original: *kompassen*. In this period, the term could refer to sundials used to determine location via the sun's shadow.</note>, and what else belongs here, using mathematical principles for every place. But the other <note>Chorography</note>, applying no property of Celestial things to the task, measures the World by paces and miles, and distinguishes it by *mountains*, *forests*, *lakes*, *rivers*, *seas and shores*. It points out the races and peoples, the kingdoms, the landscapes, the cities, the harbors, and those things that are particularly worthy of note,

> The lands' traditional use, and how they are divided;
> What fruits each province grows, or what is not provided.

And through a certain imitation of the art of painting, it represents the whole world on a globe, or a flat map <note>original: *tafel*, meaning a table or tablet.</note>, according to the principles of *Geometry* and *Perspective* <note>original: *Doorschouwing*, a literal translation of the Latin *perspectiva*.</note>.

(a) *Degrees and minutes*. (b) *Poles*.

# *Of Astrology.*

## CHAPTER XXX.

<margin>(a) Abraxas <note>A mystical word used by the Gnostic Basilides; its Greek letters add up to 365, representing the days of the year and his 365 levels of heaven.</note></margin>

### of Sciences and Arts.

[...destroys divine] providence, as it teaches that everything proceeds from a force of celestial influence, and depends upon the stars with a fatalistic necessity. Furthermore, it is the advocate of vices, glossing them over as if they fell upon us from Heaven. It defiles all good arts and overthrows them; first, **Natural Philosophy** <note>original: "Weetkunde," referring here to the systematic study of the causes of things</note>, by turning the causes of things and their inner reasons into mere fictions; next, **Medicine**, by changing natural and potent remedies into idle observations and into superstitions that are wrong and deadly to both soul and body. Finally, it completely undermines laws and morals, and all the arts of human prudence, as if <term>Astrology</term> <note>original: "Starregissing," literally 'star-guessing' or 'star-steering'</note> alone should decide at what time, in what manner, and by what means something is to be accomplished. It claims to hold dominion over life, morals, and both public and private affairs, as if it had obtained authority over everything from heaven—just as if all other things that did not recognize it as their Patroness were to be considered as nothing.

It is an art, certainly, which the devils of old maintained for the deception of men and the dishonoring of Divinity. ->Of Physiognomy.<-

## CHAPTER XXXIII.

Among these, then, Physiognomy <note>original: "Gedaantkunde," literally the study of forms or shapes</note>—following nature as its leader, so it claims—boasts that it can, through the observation of the entire body, trace the inclinations of the soul and the body, as well as a person's fortune, using recognizable signs. According to these signs, it proclaims one person a child of *Saturn* or *Jupiter*, another a child of *Mars* or the *Sun*, and yet another a child of *Venus*, *Mercury*, or the *Moon*. From the constitution of the body, it estimates their birth stars, ascending gradually (as they say) from the inclinations to the causes—namely, the astrological influences <note>original: "sterregiffelijke," literally star-guessing or star-allotting</note>—from which it then rambles <note>original: "revelt," meaning to rave or speak nonsensically</note> about whatever enters its mind.

->*Of Augury and Divination.*<-

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

**Augury** <term>Wichchelarij: from the Dutch "wichelarij," referring broadly to divination, but historically rooted in the practice of interpreting omens from the behavior of birds or other natural signs</term>, which splits itself into many different kinds, is an art that was held in great esteem even in ancient times—so much so, indeed, that people accomplished nothing, regarding either public or private affairs, without first consulting the auguries. This art is very ancient and, as *Pomponius Laetus* <note>Pomponius Laetus (1428–1498) was an Italian humanist who founded the Roman Academy and was an expert on ancient Roman rituals</note> relates, it passed from the **Chaldeans** <note>a people of Mesopotamia often synonymous with ancient astronomers and magicians</note> to the **Greeks**. Among the Greeks, *Amphiaraus*, *Tiresias*, *Mopsus*, *Amphilochus* <note>original: "Afilotes"</note>, and *Calchas* <note>legendary seers and prophets of Greek mythology and the Trojan War</note> were held to be chief augurs. From the Greeks, it passed to the **Etruscans**, and from them to the **Latins**. Even *Romulus* <note>the legendary founder of Rome</note> was himself an augur and established the rule that magistrates should be chosen through the practice of augury. And *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian of the Roman Republic</note> writes that the **Aborigines** <note>the earliest inhabitants of central Italy in Roman founding myths</note> also possessed the ancient art of augury; and that *Ascanius* <note>original: "Askaan"; the son of the Trojan hero Aeneas</note>, before he led his army against *Mezentius*, took up the practice of augury. When he saw that the omens were favorable, he fought and won. Finally, the **Phrygians**, **Pisidians**, **Cilicians**, **Arabs**, **Umbrians**, **Tuscans**, and many other nations devoted themselves to augury. The **Lacedaemonians** <note>the Spartans</note> assigned an augur to assist their kings and required him to be present at public assemblies; and among the **Romans**, there was a formal guild of augurs. This art was given credibility by those who

All these types of divination have their roots and foundations in <term>astrology</term> <note>original: "Starregissing," literally "star-guessing" or "star-governing."</note> itself: for whether the body, the face, or the hand is examined; whether a dream or a phantom is seen; whether <term>augury</term> <note>original: "wichchelarij," the practice of interpreting omens from nature, such as the flight of birds.</note> or divine frenzy inspires them, they see fit to bring a map of the heavens into the matter. From these celestial meanings, together with conjectures based on resemblances and signs, they track down the meaning of the things signified. Therefore, all divinations are tied to the art and practice of astrology, which they must acknowledge as the key necessary for the knowledge of all hidden things. Consequently, they clearly demonstrate how far all these arts of divination differ from the truth, for they seize upon principles that are so obviously false and invented out of poetic levity—things that are not, nor have been, nor ever shall be. Yet they claim these are the causes and signs for those who attribute the outcomes of things to them, contrary to the <term>square truth</term> <note>original: "vierkante waarheid," an early modern idiom for a truth that is solid, perfect, and indisputable on all sides.</note>.

# On *Magic* in General.
## CHAPTER XLI.

The progression of the subject requires here that we also speak of *Magic*: for it is so closely entwined and related to <term>astrology</term> <note>original: "Starregissing," literally "star-guessing."</note> that he who maintains *Magic* without astrology accomplishes nothing at all, but is entirely off the track. <term>Suidas</term> <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> believes that *Magic* took its name and origin from the <term>Magusaeans</term> <note>An ancient Persian priestly caste.</note>; it is the common opinion that it is a Persian word, which <term>Porphyry</term> and <term>Apuleius</term> <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who explored the relationship between the material and spiritual worlds.</note> agree upon, and that in their language it signifies the same as Priest, Sage, or Philosopher. *Magic*, then, encompassing all Philosophy, Natural Science, and Mathematics, also adds the power of Religion to them: because of this, it also includes Sorcery and <term>Incantation</term> <note>original: "Belezing," the practice of reading or chanting spells to influence the natural world.</note> within itself. For this reason, most people divide *Magic* into two kinds, namely natural and ceremonial.

---

## CHAPTER XLVII.

But here I am met with the words of *Pliny* <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (23–79 AD), a Roman author and natural philosopher. This reference is from his *Natural History*, Book 30.</note>, where he says: *there is yet another faction of Magic, namely that originating from the Jews, Moses, and Latopea* <note>original: "noch isser een andere Magice opwerping, namentlijk van de Joden, Moizes en Latopea afkomstig." In Pliny's original Latin, he mentions "Iannes" and "Lotapea" (likely a corruption of a name like Jochabed or a contemporary of Moses) as Jewish magicians.</note>: which words put me in mind of the *Kabbalah* <note>From the Hebrew *Qabbalah*, meaning "reception" or "tradition."</note> of the *Jews*; regarding which, there is a pervasive opinion among the *Hebrews* that it was given by God to *Moses* himself on Mount *Sinai*, and thereafter it was handed down only by word of mouth through a succession of memories, without the record of letters. Just as in former times the *Pythagorean* doctrines of *Archippus* and *Lysis* <note>Two of the few survivors of the destruction of the Pythagorean school in Italy, who were credited with preserving the master’s oral teachings.</note>—who kept schools in *Thebes* in *Greece*—were passed along, where the pupils, memorizing the lessons of the teachers by heart, used wit and memory in place of books. <meta>This page continues the critique of Natural Philosophy initiated on page 168. Agrippa moves from a general introduction to a specific attack on the origins of philosophy, arguing that it is rooted in the "fables" of poets and characterized by perpetual, unresolved disagreement between various schools of thought.</meta>

<header>of the Sciences, and Arts.</header>

First of all, the Poets have made profession of it, among whom **Prometheus**, **Linus**, **Musaeus**, and **Orpheus**, and finally **Homer**, are counted as the first inventors. But what truth will come to light from **Philosophy** <note>original: "Wijzgeerte"</note>, which itself has been hatched from the trifles and fictions of the poets? That this is so, **Plutarch** asserts with clear evidence; namely, that all the branches of the **Philosophers** <note>original: "Wijzgeeren"</note> have taken their origin from **Homer**. Even **Aristotle** admits that philosophers are by nature **Fable-mongers** <term>Quakgeren: A term used here to mean those who traffic in trifles or quackery; Agrippa uses it to suggest that philosophers deal in fictions rather than solid facts.</term>, that is, intent on fables. Some have split the branches of the **Philosophers** into nine, others into ten, but **Varro** into a far greater number. If one were to gather all the **Philosophers** together, they still would not be able to agree on which sect is the best, or whose doctrines one ought most to follow? Thus they bicker and split hairs with one another about every point, and they feed this dispute continually, century after century; and (as **Firmianus** <note>Lactantius Firmianus (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero," who frequently criticized pagan philosophy.</note> says) every sect undermines all the others, so that it and its own affairs may remain standing: and not one, from top to bottom, will suffer another to be called wise, lest it be forced to confess that it is itself foolish. And since **Philosophy** <note>original: "Wijſgerigheid"</note> reasons and speculates about everything, it proceeds with certainty in nothing: whether I should therefore place the **Philosophers** among the beasts or among men, I certainly do not know! They seem to be somewhat better than beasts because they have reason and wit—

## *On the Principles of Natural Things.*
### CHAPTER L. <note>Chapter 50.</note>

**F**or first, concerning the *Principles of natural things* <term>Principles of natural things: Referred to in Latin as "physica," this field sought the fundamental "archē" or first substance from which the universe was made.</term>, upon which this entire power is built, there is a fierce quarrel among the most prominent *Philosophers* <note>original: "Wijsgeren"</note>, and the lawsuit still hangs as to who among them has hit the mark best; they bring forth powerful, moving, and irrefutable reasons for contradictory things. For *Thales of Miletus* (judged the first Sage by the Oracle) maintained that all things consist of water. His listener and follower in the school, *Anaximander*, said that the principles of things are infinite. Yet his own pupil *Anaximenes* makes air the infinite principle of things. *Hipparchus* and *Heraclitus the Ephesian* [choose] fire. *Archelaus the Athenian* agrees with both of these to some extent. *Anaxagoras of Clazomenae* makes infinite principles, like small and jumbled fragments <note>Anaxagoras's theory of "seeds" or "homoeomeries," which are the fundamental building blocks of matter.</note>, but which were afterwards brought into their order by a Divine governance. *Xenophanes* asserts that everything is one, and that same thing is immovable.

Parmenides posits the hot and the cold, such as fire, as that which moves, and the earth, which gives form: *Leucippus*, *Diodorus*, and *Democritus* [posit] the full and the empty: *Diogenes Laertius* the air, yet participating in a Divine motion: *Pythagoras of Samos* established number as the principle of things, whom *Alcmaeon of Croton* follows in this: *Empedocles of Agrigentum* [posits] strife and friendship, and the four elements <term>Four elements: Earth, water, air, and fire; the standard building blocks of matter in ancient Greek science.</term>. *Epicurus* [posits] the (a) atoms <note>original: "stippen," literally "dots" or "points," referring to the Greek "atomos"</note> and the void: *Plato* and *Socrates* [posit] God, the forms <note>original: "schetzen," referring to Plato's Theory of Ideas/Forms</note>, and matter: *Zeno* [posits] God, matter, and the elements: *Aristotle* [posits] matter, as required by the form, through a certain entelechy <term>Entelechy: Translated here from "eigen voogdelijkheid" (own stewardship/governance); in Aristotelian philosophy, it is the vital force that turns potential into reality.</term> which he places as the third among the principles, contrary to what he taught elsewhere—that pluralities of things should not be counted; wherefore other younger *Peripatetics* <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>, in place of entelechy, have posited a motion that compels both things. Yet if that motion be accidental, how shall it be the principle of its own stability, or who shall be the mover of this motion? Therefore the *Philosophers of the Hebrews* have posited matter, form, and spirit.

But *Themistius* <note>A 4th-century Greek statesman and philosopher</note> says that *Aristotle* defined the active mind as one, but the understanding <note>or "passive"</note> mind as multiple, and both of these as everlasting. ...dare to say, which, as I have said, brought about the unity of the intellect <note>The "Unity of the Intellect" is a philosophical doctrine, often associated with Averroes, suggesting that all humans share a single, universal intellect</note>. The *Manichaean heretics* <note>A dualistic religious movement founded by the prophet Mani, which viewed the world as a struggle between light and darkness</note> said that one soul alone was the soul of all, or of the Universe, divided into every body, both animate <note>original: "zielige"</note> and inanimate; but those things that appear to us as inanimate participated less, and the animate more, yet the heavenly bodies most of all; and thus they finally conclude that each individual soul is nothing but a part of the universal soul. *Plato* also constructs a soul of the Universe; yet he claims that the fragmented Universe, as if separated from its soul, is animated in another way, and the pieces are also animated in a divided fashion. Furthermore, others claim one kind of soul; others not one, but two—a rational and an irrational one; others many, even as many as there are kinds of animals. The *Physician Galen* <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), an influential Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medical science for centuries</note> is of the opinion that there are various souls according to the species; moreover, he also places many souls within a single body. There are also those who place two souls in man: a sensitive one from the procreative faculty, and an intellectual one from the creative faculty; among whom is *Ockham* the theologian <note>William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), known for his development of nominalism</note>. *Plotinus* <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of antiquity and the founder of Neoplatonism</note> asserts the soul to be one thing and the intellect another; whom *Apollinaris* follows. Some do not distinguish the intellect from the soul, but say the same is the principal part of the soul's substance <note>original: "zelfftandigheid"</note>. ### [*On Moral Philosophy.*] <note>The original Dutch title is "Zeder-vormende Wijjsgerigheid," literally character-forming or moral philosophy.</note>

# LIV. Chapter.

Furthermore now, if there is (as some would have it) any *philosophy* or discipline concerning morals, I believe that it exists not so much through the clever tricks of the *philosophers*, but rather through various usage, custom, observation, and the preservation of common life, and is changeable according to the disposition of times, places, and people. It is taught to children through threats and flattery, and to the elderly through laws and punishment. A natural liveliness imparts certain things to men that cannot be taught, but which, over the course of time and through the social gathering of men, grow great through right or force. ### *Of Feast Days.*
## CHAPTER LIX.

Likewise, Feast Days have always been observed with great religious solemnity, among the pagans as well as the *Jews*: all of whom serve *God* on specific, set days chosen from certain times of the year. After that, the Church of the *Bohemians* also separated because they administered the thanksgiving <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> under both kinds <note>original: "onder beide gedaantens." It is therefore a villainy, in every respect, to tear apart the unity of the Church and divide the body of *Christ* for the sake of <term>indifferent matters</term> <note>original: "middelmatige... oorzaken." In theology, these are "adiaphora"—matters not essential to salvation over which Christians should not fight.</note> and all sorts of causes that do not hinder the *Christian faith* at all. A reference to Matthew 23:24.</note>. By disturbing the peace of the Church, they take to the field with those things where the damage of the schism causes more hindrance than the correction of the fault brings profit.

->Of Household Economy in General.<-

### CHAPTER LXVI.

Under the administration of the commonwealth is also included *Household Economy*; which is a *domestic commonwealth*, and nothing other than a *private Monarchy*: but its kinds are diverse: For some is *Royal* or *Courtly*; another *governor-like*, or *military* <note>original: "legerachtig", referring to the management of an army camp or military administration</note>; yet another, *common, or of the community, or of communal living, or social*; and finally another *private, or monastic*. This, then, teaches how the Wife, how the children, how the kinsmen <term>magen: an archaic term for relatives or kinsfolk</term>, how the household, how the servants are to be governed; how to protect and expand house and property; from where to pursue incomes: further, what shrewdness <term>snoekerheid: a term implying a sharp, almost predatory cleverness or craftiness, derived from "snoek" (pike)</term> to observe in taxation, in the circulation of money, in freightage, in leases, in tithes, in rents, in usury, in monopolies <note>original: "koopmanschappen die men alleen heeft", literally trades that one has alone</note>, and what profit is to be made there, and what sort of lease from new levies and inventions: moreover also of partnerships, of alliances, disputes and war: all of which, since they have neither measure nor rule, are therefore called lawless. Wherefore *Household Economy* may rightly be called neither art nor science, but a certain...

### *On the Ladies-in-Waiting.*
## CHAPTER LXXI.

The *Ladies-in-waiting* <note>original: "Hofjoffers," referring to the young noblewomen or attendants serving a queen or princess.</note> also have their flaws; for not a few are found with bodily gifts and an outstandingly striking appearance—haughty, radiant, and graceful, adorned in purple and gold robes and half-jewels; but not everyone wishes to see what shameful monsters often hide beneath these beautiful shells. For this reason, *Lucian* <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125 – 180 AD), a Greek satirist known for mocking hypocrisy and organized religion.</note> aptly compares them to the *Egyptian Temples*: for there, the building is very elegant on the outside, and even magnificent, built and raised with precious stonework; yet if you search further within for the *Idol*, you shall find either an *Ape*, or a *Stork*, or a *Goat*, or a *Cat*. Thus it is with the *court damsels* and *ladies*, who from childhood in their tender years are raised in velvet idleness, dancing, and all manner of wantonness, and are steeped in corrupt exercises from those *courtly love-books* <note>Likely referring to popular chivalric romances or "Books of Hours" turned toward secular romance, which Agrippa viewed as morally corrosive.</note>, and those most shameful stories of lust, of pleasure, of adultery, of intrigues, of matchmaking, farces <note>original: "pottspelen," referring to low-brow or slapstick comedic plays.</note>, novelties, buffoonery, and songs, as if they had sucked from their nurse’s breasts the most ruinous habits: fickleness, wantonness, boldness, peevishness, shamelessness, filthiness, contentiousness, contra—

## Of *Commerce*.

### CHAPTER LXXII.

*Commerce* is a cunning instigator of secret profits, a harsh whirlpool of public robbery, never happy through the joy of possession, but always miserable through the desire of seeking. Yet, many have judged that it provides no small assistance to the commonwealth <note>original: "Gemeintenstaat," referring to the state or public community.</note> and is useful for joining together the friendship of foreign kings and nations, and is also beneficial and somewhat necessary for the common life of men. Indeed, <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and naturalist.</note> Pliny even believes that it was invented for the sake of survival. For this reason, many illustrious and simultaneously wise men did not disdain to try their hand at it; among whom, as <note>Plutarch (c. 46–119 AD), a Greek biographer and philosopher.</note> Plutarch testifies, were <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–548 BC), one of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> Thales, <note>Solon (c. 630–560 BC), the Athenian lawmaker.</note> Solon, and <note>Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BC), the famous Greek physician.</note> Hippocrates. 

But just as we permit some sciences and arts for their pleasantness, value others for their activity, follow others for their virtue and honor, and respect others for their truth and justice, yet all these—though necessary, profitable, delightful, and industrious—are not therefore immediately honorable, laudable, and just. Thus also the dealings of merchants, peddlers, usurers, money-shufflers <note>original: "wiffelaars," likely referring to speculators or those who profit from shifting exchange rates.</note>, and brokers are necessary, useful, and industrious, yet they are called "unfree, foul, and unpious" gain <note>original: "onvrij, vuil, en onvroom gewin."</note>. This is because their elaborate deceits, rather than true arts, are what are bought and sold; which indeed...
