->### Of Stewardship.<-
## CHAPTER LXXIII.

Not much better than the merchants are the *Stewards* <term>original: *Rentmeeſters*—officials appointed to manage the estates, revenues, and financial accounts of a lord or a state</term>, a thieving breed of people; they are usually slavish, salaried, or those who let themselves be hired for a sum of money. They are unskilled and lazy, yet bold and impudent, possessing nothing but some meager sciences—which are the only things such people care to know—namely writing and arithmetic. But most of all, they have mastered the rather clever little tricks of stealing, acting more skillfully than the highwaymen who operate on the public roads. Consequently, they are the most thievish of all men alive, becoming wealthy only by the use of their hands, with which they count *Talents* <note>An ancient unit of weight and value, here used to signify immense sums of money.</note> and *Millions*. Their fingers are so sticky, and so equipped with endless crooked grappling hooks, that all money—however light, however fleeting, however slippery and smooth like eels and snakes—immediately sticks to them upon being touched and is not easily loosened. In this, however, they are somewhat less blameworthy: partly because they only lay snares for the treasuries of *Kings*, *Princes*, and *the Mighty*; and partly because they are not unwilling to squander what they secretly smuggle out <term>original: *lorrendrajen*—to trade illicitly or embezzle</term> on harlots, at the dice-table, on banquets, on buildings, and in feeding sycophants <note>Original: *panlikkers*—literally "pan-lickers," referring to parasites or hangers-on who flatter for a free meal.</note>, horses, dogs, and court entertainers. ->*Of Agriculture.*<-

# LXXIV. CHAPTER.

**Agriculture** then, to which *Pasturage*, *Fishing*, and *Hunting* <note>original: *Weierij*—referring to the management of game and hunting grounds.</note> are linked, was held in such high esteem among the ancients that neither the *Roman Emperors*, nor the mightiest *Kings* and *Commanders* felt it a source of shame or annoyance to till fields, to tend seed, or to graft trees. To these pursuits did *Diocletian* <note>Roman Emperor (r. 284–305 CE) who famously abdicated and retired to his palace in Salona to grow cabbages.</note> betake himself after laying down the *Imperial dignity*; as did *Attalus* <note>Attalus III, the last King of Pergamon (r. 138–133 BCE), who was more interested in botany and gardening than in ruling his kingdom.</note> after leaving the administration of his *Kingdom*. *Cyrus* also, that great *King* of the *Persians*, used to boast frequently when showing his gardens to friends who came to visit him, that they were planted by his own hands, and that he had set the trees in their rows with his own hand. Even *Seneca* <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE–65 CE), the Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note> planted *pine tree cuttings*, dug *fish ponds* with his own hand, and constructed *aqueducts*; he was nowhere more content than on his *country estates*. It is from these activities that the surnames of the noble houses—the (a) *Fabii*, the (b) *Lentuli*, the (c) *Ciceroni*, and the (d) *Pisoni*—originated, namely from the abundance of these specific field crops.

## Of Fishing.
# CHAPTER LXXVI.

To this are added *Fishing* and *Fish-farming*. The pursuit of fishing was held in such high regard and fame among the *Romans* that they brought foreign *fish*, unknown to the *Italian* shores, from distant *provinces* and released them from ships into the *Italian* sea, just as one sows seeds in the earth; they believed that no small benefit to the *Commonweal* lay in this. Furthermore, they constructed *fish-canals* and ponds, full of precious fish, at great expense. ### *Of Nobility.*
## Chapter LXXX.

From war, therefore, inherited nobility has its origin: namely, a distinction obtained from blood and the defeat of enemies through a brave butchery <note>Dutch: 'vleeschkapperij', literally 'meat-chopping'; a scathing description of combat</note>, and glorified with public honors <term>Eerlievreyen: ceremonial liveries or displays of honor</term>: from this come the many types of crowns among the **Romans**: **mural crowns** <note>given to the first soldier to scale an enemy wall</note>, **siege crowns** <note>given to a commander who broke a siege</note>, **naval crowns**; **so many military gifts, bracelets, spears, plumes, collars, rings, statues, and images**, with which the first principles of Nobility were inaugurated: among the **Carthaginians**, they were gifted with as many rings as the number of battles they had been in: the **Iberians** erected as many obelisks <term>grafnaaldens: literally 'grave-needles' or stone monuments</term> around the grave of the deceased as the number of enemies he had destroyed: among the **Scythians**, at a famous banquet, only those who had killed an enemy were permitted to toast from the communal cup: among the **Macedonians** there was a law, that those who [had] not [killed] an enemy...

# Of the Uncertainty and Vanity [of the Sciences],

In former times, none were more pleasing to the people, nor were greater rewards deemed worthy, than those who slew tyrants, their instigators, their servants, or even their innocent children. Indeed, even the *legal scholars* taught that sometimes the innocent may be lawfully killed if such an act is greatly beneficial to the *commonwealth*, or so that once the tyrant is suppressed, his children might be crushed to ensure no new usurpation of power sprouts from them. In the same way, after the overthrow of *Ilium* <note>The ancient city of Troy.</note>, the Greeks killed Hector’s heir *Astyanax*, so that no cause remained to take up a new war. 

Let us read the historians of ancient times: *Titus Livius*, *Josephus*, *Hegesippus* <note>original: "Egezip"</note>, *Quintus Curtius*, *Suetonius* <note>original: "Zuetoon"</note>, *Tacitus*, *Serenus*, *Tranquillus* <note>The author likely refers to Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus as two separate people or cites another source.</note>, and others. It was always permitted to lay traps for tyrants; it was permitted to deceive them; it was most honorable to kill them, or even to dispatch them with poison. This is how *Tiberius*, the third Emperor counting from *Julius* [Caesar], was put to death. But though poisoning has always been held as accursed, the world has nonetheless judged the poison that subdued him to have been "life-giving" <note>In the sense that the death of the tyrant brought life back to the state.</note>. 

The Holy Scriptures also agree on this regarding *Eglon*, *Sisera* <note>original: "Sifara"</note>, and *Holofernes*, whom *Ehud* <note>original: "Ajoth"</note>, *Jael*, and *Judith* slew. These acts were permitted by God’s providence, even when accomplished through a "wicked deed" <note>Referring to the violent or deceptive nature of the assassinations.</note>, killing the tyrants to throw off the yoke of oppression. But let us proceed from War and Nobility to **Medicine** <term>Geneeskonst</term>, which itself is also an art of **manslaughter** <note>Original: "menschemoorderij," literally "men-murdering." From this, a quarrel has arisen between the *Physicians* and the *Jurists* <term>Rechtsgeleerden</term>; for the Physicians argue—since "goods" are threefold in order: of the *soul*, of the *body*, and of *property* (the Theologian cares for the first, the Physician for the second, and the Jurist for the third)—that from this, the middle seat rightfully belongs to the *Physicians* above the Jurists, insofar as the body’s strength and health is better than *property* and *riches*. 

But this dispute was settled by a certain arbiter with a comical question; for he asked these contentious men: what custom and manner was observed in leading criminals to judgment? Who went first, and who followed: the thief or the executioner? When they answered that the thief went first and the executioner followed, he gave his verdict: "Let then the Jurists go first, and the Physicians follow," thereby stinging the excessive plundering of the former and the reckless manslaughter of the latter. <note>The joke implies that Jurists are like thieves who steal property, while Physicians are like executioners who finish off the person.</note>

Being unable to distinguish between these things, they place their trust in foreign merchants who ruin everything with fraud and adulteration. 

Here I could also include their harmful disagreements regarding the knowledge of simple medicines which they use, and their errors concerning the names of things in the medical art <term>medical art|original: "geneeskonst"</term>, which are poorly understood and even more poorly applied by them; a view which **Nikolaas Leoniceener** <note>Niccolò Leoniceno (1428–1524), an Italian humanist and physician who famously corrected botanical and linguistic errors in classical texts like Pliny’s Natural History.</note> points out in a lengthy book. I also refrain from mentioning the monstrous concoctions and mixtures of many foreign ingredients, from which—by scrambling everything together—they try to convince us they will produce a medicine that harmonizes with every nature (as they claim regarding the preparation of **Theriac** <term>Theriac|original: "Triakel," a legendary "cure-all" containing dozens of ingredients</term>, the fabrication of that mixture, and the **Mithridatic antidote** <note>Mithridate: a semi-mythical remedy against all poisons, named after King Mithridates VI of Pontus.</note>). ### of Sciences and Arts.

->*The supple with the hard; the weighty with the hollow.*<-

Granted, it may be so; that certain well-known mixtures <note>original: "faamenkneedingen," referring to traditional medicinal compounds or recipes passed down by reputation</note> invented by the ancient *physicians*, and found useful, may be accepted as proven; yet they are far from the true Direct Way <note>Referring to the "compendious" or efficient method of treatment, often contrasted with long-winded traditional polypharmacy.</note> and are condemned by the *physicians* themselves, being burdened by their own consciences. They have been thoroughly rejected in all the writings of *Pliny*, *Theophrastus*, *Plutarch*, *Hippocrates*, *Galen*, *Dioscorides*, *Erasistratus*, *Celsus*, *Scribonius*, and *Avicenna*. Adding their words here would take too long; they have been examined and dismissed not only by these ancients but also by many later figures. One among them, **Arnold van Nieuwen-hof** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous medieval physician and alchemist who advocated for simpler medicines.</note>, states among his maxims that when simple remedies are judged useful, it is a deception if someone uses a compound mixture. 

But nowadays, the "simples" <term>simples|original: "eenvoudige," referring to medicines made of a single herb or ingredient</term> are neglected and not even known; medicines are taken only from those two "beacons" of the herbalists <term>herbalists|original: "kruidmengers," literally "herb-mixers," a term often used for apothecaries</term> and the treasury of the perfumers—namely **Mesue** <note>Johannes Mesue, an influential medical authority in the Islamic world whose works were standard for medieval European pharmacy.</note> and **Nicolaus** <note>Nicolaus Salernitanus, author of the Antidotarium Nicolai, a foundational text for apothecary compounds.</note>—as well as other makers of antidotes. From their painted and gilded labels, all medicines are taken. 

And from this it follows that while those *physicians* attend to their leisure, directing human lives through trust in the herbalists, and these herbalists—lacking literacy and knowledge, and trusting foreign merchants—mix everything together for the convenience of their shops, there is far more danger to be expected from the medicine than from the disease. ## Of Uncertainty and Vanity;

...ness <note>This page begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page's discussion of how artificial compounds are made to resemble natural substances.</note> are imitated so convincingly that they deceive even the cleverest people; it would greatly advance the welfare of men and the commonwealth to entirely reject all those foreign and strange drugs <term>drugs|original: "droguen," referring to raw medicinal ingredients</term> which, moreover, are brought in at such a high price by those vultures, the merchants, to the detriment of the public state. It would be better to compel the *physicians* by an agreement, to banish the druggists, and to prescribe a law for them—such as one reads that *Nero* (during the time when he was still of a better nature) formerly enacted in Rome—by which they are forced to use only those medicines that our own countryside <term>countryside|original: "Landouw," referring to local fields or native terrain</term> produces. These agree better with our own natures and also come to our hands much fresher, more select, and with less difficulty and cost. 

Furthermore, local plants are subject to less danger than foreign ones, a great portion of which are held in suspicion; they are often falsified, moldy, discarded, smothered in the ship’s hold, soaked in the bilge water, or withered by old age. Often, they were not even gathered at the proper time or place (from which much danger frequently arises). For instance, the unripe *Colocynth* <note>original: "Coloquinte"; the bitter apple, a powerful and potentially dangerous purgative.</note> draws out blood and kills, and that which grows alone or in small clusters is poisonous. Likewise, the *male agaric* <note>original: "manneken-agarikum"; a wood-decay fungus used in traditional medicine.</note> is deadly, and the older it is, the more harmful it becomes. All *Scammony* <note>original: "Scammonea"; a resin used as a laxative, often adulterated in the early modern period.</note> is falsified; likewise, no reliance can be placed on *Lemnian Earth* or *Sealed Earth* <term>Sealed Earth|original: "Terra-sigillata," a medicinal clay from the Mediterranean, stamped with a seal to "guarantee" authenticity, though frequently forged.</term>. But pray, what necessity is there to use these foreign things, if our own countryside produces things of equal power and effect...

of Sciences, and Arts. 401

[men] of old practiced themselves in wars, and struck wounds upon one another, they began to seek remedies for the same: for they believed that what one person inflicted upon another by hand could also be healed by humans. The first inventor, then, of surgery was *Apis*, the *King* of the *Egyptians*, or as *Clement of Alexandria* <note>Titus Flavius Clemens (c. 150 – c. 215 AD), a Christian theologian who argued that Greek philosophy and Egyptian wisdom had their roots in Biblical history.</note> maintains, *Mizraim* <note>original: "Mizria"; in the Bible, Mizraim is the son of Ham and grandson of Noah, often identified as the progenitor of the Egyptians.</note>, older than this one, son of *Ham*, grandson of the great *Noah*: yet the healing of wounds was first described by *Aesculapius* <note>original: "Eskulaap"; the Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>; afterwards, *Pythagoras*, *Empedocles*, *Parmenides*, *Democritus*, *Chiron*, and *Peon* were excellent in this field. *Pliny* mentions that *Archagathus* the *Peloponnesian* was the very first to practice it in *Rome*; and that because of the cruelty of cutting and searing, he was commonly called the *Wound-Burner* <note>original: "Wondetser"; a reference to the frequent use of cautery in ancient surgery.</note>, and immediately the name was changed to *Butcher* <note>original: "vleischdief"; literally "flesh-thief," used here to mirror the Latin *carnifex*, meaning an executioner or someone who mangles meat.</note>; finally, the entire art fell into dislike and was driven out. ->CHAPTER LXXXVI.<-

Anatomy <note>original: "Ontleeding"; literally "un-limbing" or "dissecting."</note>, however, surpasses surgery in cruelty; as it is the theatrical butchery of both the Apothecaries <note>original: "Drogmengers"; literally "drug-mixers."</note> and the Surgeons <note>original: "Wondheelers"; literally "wound-healers."</note>. Tearing the human body apart, they search through and pry into the *site, the position, the measure, the workings, the nature of every limb, and all hidden things*, so that from this—through this cruel diligence and terrifying, horrible, and no less godless spectacle—they may learn how and in what places everything is to be healed.

### *Of Dietetics.*
<note>In this context, "dietetics" refers to the medical branch concerned with the regulation of food, drink, and lifestyle to maintain or restore health.</note>

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.

THERE remains the dietary art of medicine, whose chief advocate, above others, was *Asclepiades* <note>Asclepiades of Bithynia (c. 124–40 BC), a Greek physician who practiced in Rome and rejected the use of harsh drugs in favor of diet, massage, and exercise.</note>, who, by largely abolishing the use of drugs, brought the entire art of healing down to the manner of sustenance, to the quantity and nature of foods, and the preparation of side-dishes. From him, other *Physicians* differ not at all, but rather, believing that one requires the other, they sometimes command diet in place of drugs, and likewise drugs in place of the manner and measure of sustenance. From this they command, forbid, scold, and accuse the food and drink which God has created, and forge unsustainable rules of living; and the food, which they command others to taste only in tiny morsels, they themselves devour like pigs devouring acorns. The laws of living which they prescribe to others, they themselves are the very first to violate—not so much out of carelessness, but rather by design. For if they themselves had to live according to these dietary decrees of theirs, they would perceive a significant loss to their own health; yet, if they allowed the sick to live according to the laws of nature, just as they themselves live, they would suffer a financial loss. But concerning these diet-measurers <note>original: "eet-ijker," a derogatory term for one who strictly and pedantically gauges every bite of food.</note>, *Ambrose* <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), a Doctor of the Church.</note> speaks thus: "the commands of the remedy are contrary to divine opportunity, for they call one back from fasting, they do not permit night vigils, and they lead one away from the purpose of contemplation."

### CHAPTER LXXXIX.

The **Art of Cookery**, then, is very convenient, and not dishonest, provided it does not exceed the bounds of moderation: and this reasoning has moved even eminent and most restrained men to not be ashamed of writing about the *Art of Cookery* and the preparation of side-dishes; among the Greeks: *Pantaleon, Mithaecus, Epiricus, Zophon, Hegesippus, Paxamus, Epaenetus, Heraclides the Syracusan, Tyndaricus the Sicyonian, Simmonactides of Chios, and Glaucus the Locrian*; among the Romans: *Cato, Varro, Columella, and Apicius*; and among the later writers: *Platina* <note>Bartolomeo Sacchi (1421–1481), known as Platina, author of the first printed cookbook, "On Rightful Pleasure and Health."</note>. 

But the *Asiatics* <note>Referring to the inhabitants of Asia Minor, whom Roman moralists often blamed for introducing luxury and decadence to Rome.</note> have always been so excessive and immoderate in these matters that their very name has been turned into a surname for gluttons and gourmands, whom we therefore call *slampampers* <note>original: "slampampers," an old Dutch term for revelers, gluttons, or those who live a dissolute life of luxury.</note>. From this (as *Titus Livius* <note>Livy, the Roman historian.</note> relates), after the Asian Victory, foreign extravagances burst forth into the Roman city; for then banquets began to be prepared with greater care and costliness. It was then that an old cook—once a most despised serf—began to be held in esteem, in use, and in value; and from the kitchen, greasy as he was, dripping with fat, and crusted with chimney soot, he was received into the schools with his pots, dishes, pestle, mortar, and roasting spit. What had once been a despised servitude began to be considered an Art, whose entire concern is to gather "throat-itchings" <note>original: "keeljeukernijen," a vivid Dutch term for delicacies that tickle the palate or provoke gluttony.</note> from everywhere into a

However, the fame and renown of this art has been claimed above all others by **Apicius** <note>Marcus Gavius Apicius, the most famous gourmet of the Roman world, whose name became synonymous with luxury.</note>, so that after his name (as **Septimius Florus** <note>A Roman poet and historian.</note> testifies) the nickname of "Apicians" was passed down to cooks; by this title, they were called **Apicians** in a sort of imitation of the naming of philosophical schools. Of him, **Seneca** has written thus: "*Apicius* (he says) lived in our memory; he, in this city (from which at one time the Philosophers were ordered to depart as corrupters of youth), presenting the science of the cook-shop with his teaching, has poisoned the age." **Pliny** also quite sharply called him the deepest whirlpool of all spendthrift-gluttons. Finally, so many "ticklings of the throat," so many enticements of lust, and so many varieties of sauces have been devised and prepared by the ingenuity of these **Apicians**, that it eventually became necessary, with prescribed laws,

Flaccus** <note>Lucius Valerius Flaccus, a Roman statesman and associate of Cato the Elder.</note> and his colleague, being Censors <term>Tuchtmeesters: Roman officials who oversaw public morality</term>, expelled **Duronius** from the senate because he, as a (b) Tribune of the People <term>Zegsman des volks: *Tribunus plebis*, an official elected to protect the interests of the commoners</term>, sought to repeal the law given against the profligacy of banquets.

O, how shamelessly did **Duronius** climb the (c) Rostra <term>Bovenpeui: the *Rostra*, the elevated platform in the Roman Forum used for public speeches</term> to utter these words! "Bridles have been cast upon you, **O Quirites** <note>original: "Quiriten," a formal address for Roman citizens in their civil capacity.</note>, in no way to be endured; you people are bound and shackled to a bitter bond of servitude; for a law has been enacted which commands you to be sober! Arise! Let us cast off this dominion encrusted with the foul rust of antiquity; for what use is liberty if it is not free to those who wish to wallow in excess?" 

There were many other such arbitrary acts which are now all altered or entirely abolished, so that never has anyone provided for the gullet with more fuss and excess than in these times of ours. For this reason (as (d) **Musonius** <note>Gaius Musonius Rufus (c. 30–101 AD), a Stoic philosopher known as the "Roman Socrates."</note> and after him our **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the Church Father, who often wrote against the vice of gluttony.</note> says), we treat our bellies as (d) **Lakes and Sea-reefs** <note>original: "Lacus en Zee deurrotsen," likely a metaphor for the vastness and danger of the belly's appetite, or perhaps referring to the origins of the expensive foods consumed.</note>; and to grease the same with mead, wine, and costly food, we expend all the sweat of our lives. In our time, there are so many roast-shops, so many taverns, so many dens of sloth and brothels, wherein the people are corrupted through gluttony, drunkenness, and lustfulness.

# OF THE UNCERTAINTY AND VANITY
## OF SCIENCES AND ARTS.

I believe that King *Amasis* <note>Amasis II, a Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty of Egypt, known for laws requiring citizens to declare their income.</note> once gave a law, by which everyone was forced to give an account to the appointed authorities of what business he supported himself with; and whoever would not do so, fell into capital punishment. Though I could say many more things about this art (which, however, is not so very much against my heart), were it not for the oath of silence (which those who are initiated into these secrets are accustomed to take). This silence, moreover, was so steadfastly and solemnly maintained by the ancient philosophers and writers, that no philosopher of established authority, or credible writer, can be found who has touched upon this art anywhere, even with a single word. ## Of Law and the Laws.
### CHAPTER XCI.

<margin>(a) *determination* <note>In a legal sense, a formal decision or conclusion reached by an authority.</note></margin>
It now remains for us to speak of *Law*, which alone boasts of being able to distinguish between the true and the false, the equitable and the inequitable, the right and the wrong. Of this power, the champions in our time are the *Pope* and the *Emperor*, who boast that they have all *laws* hidden in the casket of their breasts <note>A translation of the Latin legal maxim *Omnia jura habet in scrinio pectoris sui*, implying that the ruler is the living embodiment of the law and his will is absolute.</note>, for whom the will alone is sufficient reason. ## Of Scholastic Theology.
### Chapter XCVII

Finally, it remains for us to speak of Theology. I shall pass over the theology of the pagans, described of old by *Musaeus*, *Orpheus*, and *Hesiod*, which is clearly entirely poetic and fictional—which *Eusebius*, *Lactantius*, and other Christian teachers have long since driven from the field with the most concise arguments. Nor shall I speak of the theology of *Plato* and the other *Philosophers*, all of whom we have shown above to be teachers of errors. Rather, let our discourse here be only of the Theology of Christians. It is certain that this depends on nothing but the faith of its Teachers, since it cannot be entangled with any [secular] art. 

So let us first speak of *Scholastic Theology*, that of the *Sorbonne of Paris* <note>The theological faculty of the University of Paris, then the most powerful authority in Catholic orthodoxy.</note>, which has been cobbled together from a certain mixture of divine idioms and philosophical reasons into a dual-natured exercise like the race of Centaurs <note>Agrippa uses the image of the Centaur—half-man, half-horse—to describe Scholasticism as a "monstrous" hybrid of holy scripture and pagan logic.</note>. Otherwise, however, it is very full of judgment and intellect, and has brought such great benefit to the Church in ensnaring heretics. Its inventors, and those who excelled in it, were the *Master of Sentences* <note>Referring to Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose "Four Books of Sentences" was the standard textbook for medieval theology.</note>, *Thomas Aquinas*, and *Albert* sur-

### CHAPTER XCVIII.

Interpretive theologians believe that just as grapes, olives, grain, flax, and similar fruits grow and ripen through the bounty of nature—from which, finally, through man’s ingenuity and effort, wine, oil, bread, and linen are made, thus completing the works of nature through human arts—so also the Divine Oracles <term>Orakelen: The inspired utterances or revelations from God found in the Bible.</term> are given to our interpreters to explain, because they are so obscure and hidden. This is not accomplished by our own powers or inventions, as if the Oracles of God required our help in the same way the works of nature do, but rather from the *Holy Spirit of the Scriptures* himself, who distributes his gifts to all as he wills, making some *Prophets*, and others interpreters of the *Prophets*.

This Theology, then, in order to explain divine matters, does not proceed according to the manner of the *Peripatetics* <note>original: "Peripatetiken." These are the followers of Aristotle, known for using strict logic, categorization, and systematic definitions.</note>, by sketching, or dividing, or joining things together; none of these methods pertain to God, since He can neither be sketched, nor divided, nor joined. Instead, it consists of another way of knowing, which is the middle path between our own reasoning and the *Prophetic* <gloss>Vision</gloss> (a) revelation. This path is a "fitting together" of the truth with our purified intellect (just as a key fits a lock). Just as our intellect is very eager for all truths, it is also very receptive to all understandable things, and therefore it becomes a passive <note>original: "lijden." In a philosophical sense, this means the mind is "passive" or "suffering" an impression—it is an open vessel receiving the imprint of divine truth rather than actively constructing it.</note>...

<summary>This page defines Interpretive Theology not as a human invention, but as a spiritual gift that allows humans to "finish" or reveal the meaning of God's hidden word, much like a craftsman finishes the raw products of nature. It explicitly rejects the cold, logical categorization of Aristotelian philosophy in favor of a spiritual "fitting together" of truth and the human mind.</summary>

### CHAPTER XCIX.

JUST as **Prophecy** is the discourse of the **Prophets**, so is **Theology** <term>Godgeleerdheid: literally "God-learning." In this era, it referred to the study of divine truths as revealed through scripture and tradition.</term> nothing other than the tradition of the **Theologians**—that is, of those who speak with **God**. ### CHAPTER 100.

**L**ook, there you have heard how doubtful, how double-edged, how uncertain, and how full of danger all academic exercises are, such that we are forced—as far as they are concerned—not to know where truth rests. This is true even in <term>Theology <note>original: *Godgeleerdheid*; literally "God-learning"</note></term>, unless there be someone who possesses the key of knowledge and of discernment (for the chest of truth is locked, veiled with various mysteries, and closed even to the wise and the holy), through which a path might be opened for us to such a great, such an incomprehensible treasure. 

Yet this key is nothing other than the Word of God, which alone distinguishes all power and form of words, and judges which reasoning comes from the <term>art of sophistry <note>original: *woordvittige konst*; the practice of using clever but false arguments; literally "word-picking" or logic-chopping</note></term>—presenting not the truth, but merely an image of it—and which reasoning possesses the truth not in outward appearance and <note>original: *blanketsel*; refers to cosmetic makeup or white lead used to hide imperfections</note> "paint," but in its very being and reason. He who does not rest upon it, or does not agree with it, is—as <note>Referencing 1 Timothy 6:4</note> *Paul* says—puffed up, knowing nothing.

# [Of] the Sciences and Arts:

Romans gave a specific name to the *Christians*, calling them *Asses-heads*, and they even painted the image of *Christ* with *Ass's ears*; *Tertullian* <note>original: *Tertullianus*; an early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) who wrote about "Onolatry," the false accusation that Christians worshipped an ass.</note> testifies to this. For the song and the humming tunes of nightingales are of no use to *Ass's ears*, and the proverb says that the unpleasant and by no means *musical* braying of asses sounds nothing like the lyre. But nevertheless, once the marrow is pushed out of the *Ass’s* shinbones, one can make the very best flutes from them. These flutes, when played with the breath, far surpass and overcome the most fluid singing of all birds and the most excellent sounds of any *lyre* or *Cithara* <note>original: *Cÿther*; an ancient Greek stringed instrument.</note>. ### Henry Cornelius Agrippa. ###

...that I believe there is hardly a person to be found who, viewing his so very renowned writings with wonder, would not also receive the account of his life with an appreciative eye; especially, I say, one of my *countrymen*, to whom access to his *Latin loftiness* <note>original: "Latynsche Hoogdravendheid"; Agrippa wrote his major works in scholarly Latin, which was the language of the elite, often making his ideas and life story inaccessible to common Dutch readers of the time.</note> and his piecemeal, scattered *biography* is not granted. We provide here, then, such a narrative—not exactly as it connects from point to point in a perfect chain, but insofar as these letters of his and his friends have been willing to serve us, since otherwise there is little or no material at hand for this purpose. And even if a precise and complete knowledge is not achieved in everything here, it shall be according to the greatest probability and likelihood; for which reason we shall frequently let him speak with his own words, so that the reader himself may judge where they most likely lead.

*Henry Cornelius Agrippa* was born in *Cologne* on the *Rhine*, in the year Fourteen hundred eighty-six, on the 14th of the *Autumn month* <note>September</note>; the first name of his Father I have not happened to find anywhere in his writings (the surname is said to be the family of *Nettesheim* or, in our pronunciation, *Nettenheim*); likewise, I have found neither the name nor the surname of his *Mother* or maternal lineage. This much is known, however: that he calls his cousins the prominent *Nobles of Eilens*, and one *William Forbitius*; but whether this last one was related to him by blood on his mother's side, or by marriage...

The Ancients were accustomed, through a common proverb, to represent an outstanding folly by saying one "brings owls to Athens": <note>original: *Nachtuilen te Athenen brengen*—an ancient Greek idiom meaning to perform a redundant or pointless task, similar to the English "carrying coals to Newcastle."</note> it is no less a folly, and a very great godlessness, to bring Devils to hell. Hear now a matter both foolish and ungodly. It seemed good to us to insert this letter here in its entirety (as it will also be useful later) wherein we see, as if in a mirror, the state of this man’s mind regarding the practice of forbidden arts, of which he was held in suspicion. This is done so that the title of *Sorcerer*, which was later pinned upon him—and which still, whether out of malice, an outdated delusion, or perhaps ignorance, does not seem entirely erased by some—might finally vanish like smoke. We have heard him speak here in his mature years, although we had stepped away from the account of his youth, to which we now return.

Then, clambering over the peaks by a rocky passage, we came along pathless stones unaccustomed to human footsteps into the lowest valley on the level ground. This escape of ours, as I understood afterward, brought the rebellious peasants (who regarded it more as a miracle than a common wonder) into many various anxieties. For they now began to fear anxiously for themselves that the **King**, by means of the access through the unknown paths discovered by our cunning and industry, might unexpectedly send some soldiers upon them to devastate the entire valley with fire and sword as a severe retribution. But what shall we say when a spiritual person, when a *Bishop*, thus beats the drum, exchanges his Mitre for a *Helmet*, and makes his *Bishop's staff* (that is, the ancient *Roman Lituus* <note>The *lituus* was a curved wand used by Roman augurs to mark out the sky, but the word also refers to a high-pitched military trumpet</note> which the *Soothsayers* and *Priests* were accustomed to carry) appear as a clarion (that is, the *Lituus* or *Field Trumpet* of the *Roman Commanders*)? Is it any wonder that such incitements awaken the desire of youth, and ignite the heat of the blood with double courage? 

Just as *Agrippa* testifies of himself, he did not serve the *Emperor Maximilian* sluggishly in peace or in war, nor indeed other *Kings* and *Princes*, whether in letters, in the field, or in embassies. He records that by commission of the *Emperor* he became an *Auratus Eques* <note>original: "Auratus Eques," meaning a Golden Knight or Knight Bachelor</note> <insert>Golden Knight; some translators of our time call it Knight of the Golden Spurs; though I know not why</insert>. He obtained this order not through flattering persistence, nor was it borrowed from some overseas journey, nor seized through shameless excess at the enthronement of *Kings*; rather, it was earned in public battles, in the heat of the fight, through military virtue. 

This was a dignity that was long held in such high esteem that the *Golden Knights* used to hold rank alongside the *Counts*, and above the *Bannerets* <note>original: "Baanderheeren," a rank of nobility entitled to lead a company of men under their own banner</note>. # The Life of Agrippa

...rewards of virtue, has been a high and distinguished dignity, and an outstanding honor among many peoples: the state of the *Knights*, whom they called *Golden Knights* because of the golden ornaments <note>Referring to the golden spurs and collar typically associated with this rank</note> which were given to them. To this very respectable level of honor, in ancient times, no one used to be admitted except those whose excellent deeds and renowned virtue in war made them worthy of such merit. For to such individuals alone, this honor was conferred by the *Field Commander* as a reward for dangers and a fruit of labor, with a customary state ceremony in the presence of the entire army. 

This custom, which had become entirely obsolete, was recently brought back to the fore by *Francis I, King of France* <note>Francis I (r. 1515–1547) famously sought to embody the "Knight-King" ideal</note>, when he himself, fighting bravely in that famous battle against the *Swiss* <note>The Battle of Marignano in 1515, where Francis I was knighted on the battlefield by the legendary Chevalier de Bayard</note>, among the first and the boldest, performed both the office of an excellent Commander and a brave Soldier, so that he might truly be an establisher of an illustrious and glorious example, for which he renewed the customary ceremonies according to the ancient manner, etc. 

Thus far *Junius* <note>Hadrianus Junius (1511–1575), a Dutch physician and humanist scholar</note>. That scabby race, the people of Dominic <note>The Dominican Order, also known as the Order of Preachers, founded by Saint Dominic. They were the primary inquisitors and rivals to the humanists like Agrippa.</note>:
Burn him, and those from whom he came, who in times past dared to teach
How to poison the consecrated body of the Lord <term>The Eucharist or "body of the Lord" refers to the bread used in Holy Communion.</term>,

Who sought life there, instead to his death!
To desecrate such a holy thing! Are these unknown matters,
Are they unknown, I say, these things we set out to sing?
For indeed, by no other sword than this
Was the Emperor Henry helped into the earth <note>A reference to Emperor Henry VII (c. 1273–1313), who was rumored to have been poisoned by a Dominican friar, Bernardino of Montepulciano, using a poisoned sacramental wafer during Communion.</note>,
Since at that very table, from the hands of Paulinus <note>original: "Paulinus"; likely referring to the friar or a specific account of the poisoning.</note>,
Poison and the food of life fell upon his teeth.
Now you cry out, "Does that concern us? That happened years ago!"
But it was your own cook who mixed the two together;
"Once," you say, "we did it, that must now be forgiven."
But Bern can show anew a second piece of villainy <note>Referring to the "Jetzer Affair" (1507–1509) in Bern, Switzerland, where four Dominicans were burned at the stake for faking miracles and apparitions of the Virgin Mary to gain influence over their rivals, the Franciscans.</note>,
A work of our own time; when you burned wounds into a man,
To give the appearance of holiness, and showed them in foot and hand <note>The "stigmata" or miraculous wounds of Christ, which the conspirators in Bern faked on a simple-minded tailor named Hans Jetzer.</note>
In order to silence the Brothers of Francis <note>The Franciscan Order, who were the chief theological rivals of the Dominicans.</note>,
So that no one, not even their head, would obtain those marks.
Indeed, Bern thus brought forth a fabricated oracle,
And the voice and answer of the statue of Mary was heard,
And showed the Sacrament smeared with your poison;
Vigandus <note>Likely referring to a specific Dominican preacher or polemicist involved in the controversy.</note> dared to enchant the people during his preaching
And cast out many whims concerning the original sin and defect
Of the chaste Mother-Maid <note>The "immaculate conception": the Dominicans and Franciscans famously feuded over whether Mary was born without "original sin." Dominicans generally argued she was born with sin but later purified.</note>; and brought back upon his own neck
That which he confirmed with cursing and with insults.

# Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa. 548

[...who you say I] am; for, among other things, you called me, in a large gathering, repeatedly a **judaized Heretic**, who has introduced into the Christian schools those most shameful, damned and forbidden *Cabalistic* <note>Referring to Kabbalah, a school of thought in Jewish mysticism. Agrippa and other Renaissance humanists practiced "Christian Kabbalah," believing these ancient secrets could prove Christian truths.</note> arts; who, despising the holy Fathers and *Catholic* <note>At this time, "Catholic" meant the universal, orthodox tradition of the Western Church.</note> Teachers, values the *Jewish Rabbis* no less; and who stretches and pulls the holy scriptures according to heretical arts and the *Talmud* <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, containing legal and theological discussions.</note> of the Jews. 

But I am a Christian, and neither death nor life shall separate me from the faith of Christ: I place the *Christian Teachers* above all; however, I do not despise the *Jewish Rabbis*, and if I have erred—which is possible—I do not wish to be a heretic, nor do I seek to live in a Jewish manner. As for damned and forbidden arts, it is so far from the case that I teach them, that I would not even want to learn them myself. I do not distort the Holy Scriptures anywhere, but following the explanation of various Teachers, I take their testimony now in this way, then in that. I have not taught heretical arts or Jewish errors, but a Christian and Catholic book, *On the Wonder-Working Word* <note>original: "van het Wonder-Woord"; referring to Johann Reuchlin’s 1494 book *De Verbo Mirifico*, which explored the power of divine names.</note>, by the Christian teacher *Johann Reuchlin*, explained with much labor and late-night study—not secretly in some private chambers, but in the public schools, in the public lecture hall, with open lessons, etc.

And further on: "Let it be so, that I as a youth, not yet twenty-three years old, conducted my lessons somewhat incautiously, and am to be rebuked for that (although..."

> [...it is] said that those who are perfect do not stumble in any word) <note>A reference to the New Testament, James 3:2: "If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man."</note> yet this should nonetheless have happened in an entirely different and more godly and Christian way than you have done. # Henry Cornelius Agrippa.

...knowing and understanding, if he, who is the essence and the maker of our intellect, whose image we are, is not known: therefore I have begun to write what follows concerning the knowledge of God, as being the most necessary and most desirable thing, and the stages <note>The "steps" or "stages" refer to the Neoplatonic idea of a spiritual ladder or ascent toward the divine.</note> that lead us to the same: writing less, however, than the matter itself requires; for it is not unknown to me how broad a field for writing opens up here: yet I have preferred to write in such a way that something might rather be added to it, than taken away; so that in such divine subject matter I might not, with any justice, be rebuked for being too wordy and rambling: and whoever shall judge that something more should be added to this writing of ours, I shall consider myself helped by them, rather than rebuked. And since in these previous days I have dedicated my dialogue on man <note>Referring to his work *De Homine* (On Man).</note>, who is the image of God, to your Highness, so this Oration on the knowledge of God <note>original Dutch: *Reden, van de kennisse Gods*; referring to his treatise *De Triplici Ratione Cognoscendi Deum* (On the Threefold Way of Knowing God).</note> rightfully belongs to your Highness as well: indeed, what of mine does not rightfully belong to you? No one can know the image unless he knows him whose image it is: Receive then, magnificent Prince, these writings of ours, to be a memorial of my good inclination toward you, while you provide the honor and ornament to the writings and the author. Farewell, most happily, from *Casale* <note>Casale Monferrato in the Piedmont region of Italy.</note>, in the year 1516.

It shall certainly be the supreme knowledge, the supreme godliness, and invincible justice to know and love the beginning of all things: on the contrary, there is no greater injustice, no greater impiety, than to pay no heed to the knowledge of God, and to despise the same through neglect; of which even the Pagan *Virgil* warns us with this little verse:

## The Life of

[The Swit]zers being defeated <note>original: "zers geslagen zijnde". This refers to the Swiss mercenaries who were defeated by the French forces at the Battle of Marignano in September 1515.</note>, and *Milan* being taken by force, *Agrippa* experienced a drastic turn in his status and situation (as the Emperor’s affairs here were greatly declining). He suffered no small loss of his property and books, which at that time had remained in *Milan*: here he lost, along with several other writings, his commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the *Romans*, which were completed fully up to the sixth chapter, and thereafter in fragments. This loss caused him great pain afterward, and he exerted much diligence and labor to recover them, especially when he understood they had remained in the safe-keeping of his late pupil, *Christophorus Schilling*. However, despite the exhortations he used, and notwithstanding the promises of *Christophorus*, it is not known whether he ever recovered the aforementioned Commentaries himself. 

In this turmoil of affairs, he was advised to depart from *Pavia*, to which he replied as follows: "Whether it is due to our godlessness against Heaven, or the usual influence of the heavenly bodies, or the providence of God who governs all, most learned *Augustine* <insert>[be it *Augustinus Furnarius* <note>Agostino Furnari was a celebrated jurist and colleague of Agrippa at the University of Pavia.</note> or someone else]</insert> that—given that one could hardly be safe even in the caves of the mountains because of the violence of arms and the destruction of the Soldiers raging everywhere—I do not know: but, I pray you, whither should I flee in such a dangerous storm, with my Wife, and Son, and household? She left behind a son and a daughter, who were mentioned previously. Regarding this death, he expressed a profound sorrow and had her honorably laid to rest in the Cathedral <note>original: "Hoofdkerk"</note> of *Metz*. As a testament to his cherished memory and love, he covered the grave with a carved stone. Moving from there to *Geneva* <note>original: "Gebenne" — a common 16th/17th-century spelling for Geneva</note>, he took up residence for the remainder of that year and the entire following year, either due to the state of his affairs or because he entered into marriage <note>original: "Huwelijk"</note> once again.

He acted as one who cared not a whit for the implacable wrath and eternal hatred of the King and his mother, choosing rather to suffer everything than to endure a stain on his good name or take any dishonor upon himself; for he now counted the hatred earned through virtue, and the envy gained through truth, among his titles and honors of state.

### Lights of his century.

# EPIGRAM
### By the same [author]
## ON THE LEUVEN
## BONE-SETTERS:

> The world, so that the Arts—which are gasping for air and hoping for your power with a foot upon their heart—might finally breathe again, has waited a long, long time for your master-staff, O Bone-setters <note>original: "Ledezetters"; while literally meaning those who set broken limbs, here it is used as a mocking term for the critics of Leuven who attempted to 'fix' or 'rearrange' the reputation and works of scholars like Agrippa.</note>. On one side, someone wants to plunge an Agrippa <note>original: "Agrip"; a shortened, familiar form of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa.</note> into the water; here he is threatened with the rope <note>original: "bast"; literally bark or skin, but idiomatically referring to the gallows or a hempen rope.</note>; there they speak of peat and faggots <note>original: "mutsaart"; a bundle of brushwood used to fuel the fires for burning heretics at the stake.</note>; elsewhere, one dares to doom him to hell in the dark vapors, as if to spite God: What happens? Finally, a mouse is born <note>This is a reference to the Latin poet Horace’s phrase "Parturient montes, nascetur ridiculus mus"—the mountains are in labor, but only a ridiculous mouse is born. It suggests that the critics' massive efforts produced a pathetic result.</note>. It ends in a laugh; such an attack, such fame! Thus it goes for him who shoots all his arrows in vain and aims at his superior: now you travel the world, on everyone’s tongue; go now, go provoke with your bundle of weapons and marksman’s gear, your true equals: the Cranes and the Pygmies <note>original: "Kranen en de Dwergen"; a reference to the "Geranomachia," a mythical and absurd battle from Greek legend. By comparing the critics to these figures, the author suggests their intellectual war is trivial and comical.</note>; there you shall be Emperor, and Gods, and even more.

> **L**ady *Folly dwells in every court;*
> *She dictates the Law, and reigns supreme:*
> *And the courtly drone of base-born souls*
> *Follows at her heels like a swarming hive.*
